paragraphs.text: FROM THE LIFE OF BASIL, BY GREGORY HIS DISCIPLE [?]. [P. 395] 1. The emperor Basil, surnamed the Macedonian, had four sons: Constantine, Leo, Stephen and Alexander. Of these, Constantine departed this life while still very young. Stephen was appointed archbishop of Constantinople, a man outstanding in every virtue. He too soon paid the debt of nature. He had received repeated purgings from the physicians for the inflammation that troubled him from [?], and these badly chilled his stomach, so that he fell into an illness hard to describe and died. Their father Basil had killed Michael, who reigned before him, and so had seized the sceptre. As he lay in his death agony he saw this Michael accusing him and saying, "What
did I do to you, O Basil? What wrong did I ever do you, that you killed me so mercilessly?" Confessing in this way, he came to the end of his life, leaving his sons Leo and Alexander to the throne.

2. In the tenth year of their reign, the emperors sent certain magistrianoi to Asia on some business. As these men were passing through one of the rugged mountains there, they came upon the saint, who was living on it at that time, wearing simple clothing and grown wild like one raised in the mountains. Taking him for a spy, they leapt from their horses just as they were and seized him, and took him back with them to the imperial city. [P. 395] When this was reported to the emperors, he was handed over for examination to a certain Hagarene named Samonas, a patrician by rank, so that he might learn from the man himself who he was, where he came from, and what his proper name was. 3. Samonas took him to his own house and seated himself in all his pomp (for he was fond of novelty, conceited, and puffed up by his great wealth), and at once ordered the saint to stand before his face. The saint stood there with an undaunted spirit and would not even bend the knee, as is customary before rulers. Samonas grew very angry and said to him sternly, "Answer us: who are you, where are you from, and what is your name?" But the saint did not answer him. He stood quietly, gazing at him with gentle eyes. 4. Then the saint said to him, "And who are you, and where are you from?" Samonas replied, "I am Samonas, patrician and parakoimomenos of those who now hold the sceptre of the Romans." The blessed man said to him, "And I am a stranger, one of those who sojourn on the earth." 5. Samonas said, "Most unholy of men, how long will you hide the deceit in your heart?" The blessed man said to him, "Those who secretly do the deeds of Sodom, as you do, are the ones rightly called unholy." For Samonas was a eunuch by nature and handsome to look at. 6. Leo, who then held the sceptre, passed away, and a year and a little more later his own brother Alexander also departed. Alexander left his nephew Constantine, Leo's son, as successor to the throne, together with his mother Zoe. Since the boy was a mere infant, Alexander appointed guardians and protectors for him: Nicholas, archbishop of Constantinople, John Garidas the magister, and their associates, who were to preserve the imperial rule for the child so that no one would seize it. Once these men had been entrusted with the administration of the palace, as has been said, unseemly things were done in public affairs. The barbarian nations round about took advantage of the lack of restraint and plundered the country around the city, since there was no one able

to drive them back. So the city rose up against Nicholas for not governing it properly. He and his associates then resolved to write to Constantine Doukas, who was at that time general of the East, [P. 396] asking him to come and take the sceptre of the empire in hand, with the child Constantine, born in the purple, reigning alongside him. The boy, being a child, would remain in the palace, while Doukas, as a most valiant man and highly distinguished in war, would take the field against the foreigners. And the man truly was extremely skilful and victorious. He was a wonder even to his enemies. When they were asked, as they often were, how one man could rout them, they would answer reluctantly and in shame: "Whenever this man goes out to war, fire from his weapons meets us full in the face, and likewise from the breath of his horse, burning us [?]." When he himself was asked about this, he did not conceal the gift he had been given, but said: "Once in my youth, while I was asleep, I saw a most glorious lady clad in purple, and with her a fiery horse and armour giving off fire. She pressed me to put the armour on, though I was unwilling and cowering, and likewise persuaded me to mount the horse, [saying ?]: 'Those who blaspheme God and my Son will melt like wax before your face.' Having said this, she flew away." So much for the man. 7. When those who governed the empire wrote to him about the rule, he replied that he was not equal to it. They wrote back a second time: "The whole Roman state seeks you as emperor." He put them off again, replying in writing: "It is not right for me to set myself beside the Lord's anointed, even if he is not yet of age, and so to sin before God. I am also afraid that this may be a trap, and that you mean to do away with me." When they received this letter they sent him dreadful oaths, swearing by the immaculate [?] and precious wood that they were not plotting as he supposed, but were summoning him to the throne in simplicity of heart and with guileless souls. As a pledge they also sent their own reliquaries. Trusting in these, he took his own men and set out for the imperial city. He entered it when the sun had already risen and, praised with boundless glory by those who accompanied him, went on toward the palace. But no good sign was shown at his entry; rather, it foretold the slaughter that was to come. For the most brilliant sun let drip upon the earth something like purple dye made of blood. When Nicholas and his associates saw him coming in, [P. 397] they changed their minds and shut the entrances of the palace against him. So he went and encamped in the theatre of the Hippodrome, where all the magnates who had gathered acclaimed him as emperor. But all who were attached to the saint had heard

from him three months beforehand of the deadly calamity that was to happen, and they shut themselves up in their own houses and kept quiet. From the moment he foretold it, he did not cease to groan, lament and mourn. 8. Two protospatharioi, sons of a certain magnate, came to him and asked whether it would be to their advantage to go and join the [?] of Doukas. He said to them, "No, children, do not do it, or you will suffer what cannot be undone. If you do, one of you will fall by the sword, and the other will have his ears and nose cut off and will barely escape death." They disobeyed the saint and suffered what he had foretold. For Doukas planned badly and bought evil wages for himself and those with him. He ought to have been patient and secured the entrances of the palace so that no provisions could be brought in. Then those inside, pressed by famine, would have opened the gates to him as suppliants and eagerly received him into the palace. He did not do so. Instead he took counsel with his men to enter by the gate they call the Chalke, breaking the bars with axes. First, however, he bound his men with most dreadful oaths not to draw any sword whatever against anyone, nor any arrow or spear, but to enter without shedding blood. He said, "If they slaughter us when we are not [resisting ?], we shall bring our case against them before the fearful judgement seat of the great God, because after [binding] us with oaths they are now rising against us." Having said this he came with them, as has been said, to the Chalke gate and began to go in. But those in the palace quickly gathered the archers and shot at them with arrows from the walls. When Doukas's men were struck by the missiles they shouted to him, "Let us fight back against them!" He forbade it. While they were saying this, one of the most skilled archers found out which man was Doukas, bent his bow with all his might, and struck him in the side beneath the right arm. Doukas cried out, "Woe is me, wretch that I am! We have come here to our ruin!" and at once fell to the ground. All his men were seized with fear and began to fall back. Those inside took courage, [P. 398] drew their swords, opened the gates, and rushed out at them with great eagerness. First they killed his protostrator, then many others, and after these Doukas himself. Nor did they spare the rest, but mowed them down like ears of grain as they fled and stumbled over one another. Some would have escaped, had not those merciless and heartless men sent [?] and carefully secured and sealed all the gates of the city. Then they made a careful search for the fugitives and spared none of them. Many magistroi and patricians were found to have sat with Doukas in the Hippodrome. Some of these they ordered to be put to the sword, others to be hanged on forked gallows outside the walls, others to have their eyes

gouged out, others to be hamstrung, others to be exiled. Still others, who had done no wrong at all, they ordered to be flogged, and others to have their property confiscated. One could then see the great city suffering things it would not have endured even if barbarians had conquered and captured it. 9. Those who had slain Doukas and his son cut off their heads and brought them to Nicholas, or rather, I should say, "Agricolaus", and his associates. These recognized the heads and gave no ordinary honours to those who brought them. Even so the wicked men were not satisfied, but ordered the eparch of the city to have the remains of all the slain thrown into the sea. They pitied them neither as fellow believers nor as fellow countrymen, not to mention kinsmen, so as to allow at least their bodies to be given to [burial ?]. Instead the savage beasts put them on wagons, half cut to pieces and stripped, and so dragged them through the public streets,

10. Some say that more than three thousand gave themselves up to death by refusing to draw a sword or any other blade because of the oath. Concerning those hanged on the gallows, many trustworthy witnesses testified that they often saw at night, over each one of them, a star coming down from heaven and shooting about until dawn. In this way God showed that they had committed so great a slaughter of the innocent unjustly. For once Doukas had been slain, they ought to have spared the others, who raised no hand, did not quarrel, did not cry out. But they mercilessly shed innocent blood. Alas for the wretchedness of those who did it, and woe to them on the dread day of judgement, for the Lord will require [P. 399] the blood of their brothers at their hands. 11. When the loathsome men saw the head of Doukas, as we said before, they mocked it and ordered it to be fixed on a pole and paraded through the whole city, "so that," they said, "those who set their hopes on him may be put to shame." In the end this too was given to the depths of the sea along with the rest of the body. So it perished in this manner, but his ever-memorable spirit was received into the bosom of Abraham. For, as we said, he did not set foot in the palace as a usurper, but trusting in most dreadful oaths. He could have fought with weapons, or set fire to the palace and so taken vengeance on those within, but he did not do so. He committed himself to God, and through this trial he attained the kingdom of heaven. And the guilt lies not so much with the others who guarded the palace as with the shepherd of the rational sheep, an Attila rather than a Nicholas. Oh, how he opened the Gospels with his defiled hands! How did he not hear the one who says through them, "The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep"? But acting against it... Matt. [?]; Ezek. [?]

CHRONOGRAPHY OF SYMEON, MAGISTER AND LOGOTHETE. Leo the Armenian and Iconoclast, emperor of the Romans, 7 years and 5 months. [P. 400, 401] Year of Cadmus [?], year of the divine incarnation [?]: Leo the Armenian, also called the Chameleon, the Apostate and Iconoclast, emperor of the Romans, 7 years and 5 months. He was short in stature (which is why he was also called Chameleon), [?], good-looking, with a well-set beard and thick hair, and a voice that roared like a lion's. He was bold [?]

of the Armenians. The Assyrians were named after Asshur, but the Armenians after a certain man called Armenius, who came from Armenia, a city of Thessaly, and campaigned with Jason. 2. When this Leo was crowned by the patriarch Nicephorus, he confirmed in writing that he was orthodox in faith. But the wolf hidden in the fleece did not escape the good shepherd's notice. For when the patriarch placed the diadem on that defiled head, he seemed to feel pain, as though pricked by thorns and thistles. When the customary rite had been completed, the wretch went off to the palace amid acclamations. When he reached the round porphyry marble set in the pavement before the gates of the Chalke, he gave thanks to the icon of Christ our God there, whether sincerely or for show. There he took off the garment he had put on, which shone with rose-coloured hues, the one they call the kolobion, following an ancient custom preserved among generals, and handed it to Michael of Amorion, who was his groom. When Michael put it on, those who understood such things reckoned it an omen that he would succeed Leo on the throne. Then, when they came to the so-called Skyla, Michael stepped heavily on Leo's garment and so treated it with contempt. Leo noticed this and took it as an omen that some revolt would soon befall him. 3. Then he remembered the monk living in Philomelion who, in the time of Bardanes, had told him what would happen. So he sent him votive offerings for his needs, asking for his prayers. But that monk had died in the meantime, and in his place there was another monk called Sabbatius. He had heard the former monk's words, had slipped into his cell, and was opposed to the veneration of the holy icons. When he saw what the emperor had sent, he made a show of sending it back on the ground that the emperor venerated the holy icons, and he wrote to him foretelling that because of this the Lord would overthrow his reign. Deceived by this, the emperor summoned Theodotus Kassiteras. Even before Leo seized the empire, this man had heard a woman with a spirit of Python walking about the marketplace and crying out that the general of the Anatolikon was going to take over Michael's empire. He had then taken Leo with him and gone [P. 403] to the church of Saint Paul at the Orphanotropheion, and there they made a pact with each other to keep the secret, and he told Leo to take courage, "because it has been foreknown of you by a divine vision that you will soon attain the empire." So the emperor summoned this Theodotus and showed him what had been sent back. Theodotus seized the opportunity and added evil to evil. He persuaded the emperor that a certain monk who had his dwelling at the Mauriani [?] worked wonders, proclaiming him a second Antony the Great. Having planted this idea in the emperor's mind, he went off to the monk and, as a set-up, said this to him: "Tomorrow I will bring the emperor to you in humble clothing. [?] and quickly

of his life, I advise you to tell him that [this will happen] unless he aligns himself with the doctrine of Leo the Isaurian. And that if he keeps to it he will reign for thirty-two [?] years, see his children's children on the imperial throne, and be shown to be the thirteenth of the apostles; but if not, the opposite: countless horrors and swift destruction." When night came, the emperor went with Kassiteras to the monk, and at once he was rebuffed by him, as though the monk had seen through his disguise in advance. He said, "You, who are emperor, ought not to put on a show like this in a private person's dress." Astonished at this, the emperor became obedient to him in the matter of destroying the holy icons. Straight away he vomited out the venom he held within him against true religion, and in his madness he began the heresy. 4. Looking for fellow initiates, he found John, called the Grammarian, a second Jannes, or rather a Simon, who was also named Hylilas, which in Hebrew means forerunner and co-worker of the devil. He was the son of Pankratios the shade-painter [?], had been possessed by a demon from boyhood, and was notorious for lecanomancy and obscene practices. He also found Constantine, a priest of the shoemakers' quarter [?], who had become a lawyer at the Forakiou [?]. Constantine had fled because of his crimes, become a monk, and been renamed Antony; he was a teller of tales and a buffoon who lived shamefully. He became abbot of the monastery of the Metropolitans [P. 404] and taught these things to those under him, and later, by God's permission, he even became bishop of Syllaeum. Leo found some others too who shared his views. Meanwhile a comet appeared in the form of two bright moon-like discs, which joined and separated again into various shapes, so that they even took the form of a headless man, like the one that appeared in the time of the emperor Michael the Kouropalates. Some interpreted it, saying that the headless figure was a head [?] signifying Thomas, who later rose in revolt, and the rebels with him. Moreover, terrible earthquakes, plagues, droughts and scorching heat occurred in the days of that God-hated man.

the patriarch and the bishops with him before the senate, and said: "You know well that some people have arisen saying that icons ought not to be venerated." Nicephorus, now among the saints, was the first to answer him: "The sacred icons of the saints, O emperor, are to be honoured, since they appeared from the beginning by divine assent. The holy cloth that Christ once took and laid upon his face, on which his likeness came to be without the work of hands, is to be honoured and is venerable. Then there are the icons of Christ himself and of her who bore him, painted by the holy apostles' own hands, and the icon of the Transfiguration in Rome [?]

preserved, in which Christ appeared with Moses and Elijah on Tabor; this was made at the urging of Peter, the chief of the apostles. There is also what happened in the city of Lydda in the East. There is an ancient and venerable church there, built by believers in the name of the Theotokos, in which the likeness of the Theotokos is painted. The Jews claimed it as their own. When the Mother of God heard of this in Jerusalem, she said: 'Let the church be shut and let no one go in, and on the fortieth day let it be opened. If no sign is seen in it, let the church belong to the Jews.' After the appointed time they opened it and saw the likeness of the Theotokos holding Christ as a baby in her arms. It was a wondrous form and beauty, at once most venerable and most worthy of God, on translucent slabs, clearly visible and penetrating right through into the depth of the stone. When the Jews saw it [P. 405] they fled. Afterwards many Jews and pagans tried to scrape it off but failed, and the form not made by hands remains on the slab to this day, just as it was, to the glory of God. Besides these there is also the image of the woman with the flow of blood in Paneas, [which heals] every affliction through the herb [that grows there], and is known throughout the land." 6. After him the holy Euthymius, metropolitan of Sardis, spoke boldly and silenced the wretch. Theodore, abbot of the Studios, said: "Do not unsettle the order of the Church, O emperor. To you has been entrusted the care of the state and of the army; look after these, but leave the Church alone." But the tyrant, boiling over with rage, drove them all out with insults and exiled the patriarch Nicephorus and Theodore. It is said that at that time, as the patriarch Nicephorus was being escorted into exile, Theophanes, called "of Sigriane", who was superior of the monastery of Megas Agros, saw him from far away with prophetic eyes. He burned incense, sent him on his way with prayer, raising his hands and committing him to God, and prolonged his farewell. When someone asked him the reason, he said: "See, the great confessor Nicephorus the patriarch is passing by into exile, contending for the holy icons." As for the holy Euthymius, because he had spoken his refutation of the heresy more sharply, the emperor bruised his cheeks with blows and tore his back with whips, so severely that he breathed his last under them. After this he had Theodotus Kassiteras ordained patriarch, a man without reason and more voiceless than a fish. He openly stirred up a pitiless persecution against the Church, entrusting it to his fellow initiates, who had urged him to do three things: to deny our orthodox faith, to destroy the divine icons, and to persecute the pious. First he tore down every sacred [image] set up in the churches... [Note:] "and appeared": "in which" [?]

[?]…, and from then on he condemned to dreadful punishments and to death those found to have an icon of Christ or of the saints, many of them men of rank and distinction, and also countless monks [?]. 7. Leo had honoured Michael from Amorion, whose child he had adopted as his son at the spiritual font, with the ranks of patrician and commander of the Excubitors. But Michael, with a bold tongue, reproached Leo as a destroyer of the holy icons, and said that his wife had been joined to him in an unholy marriage. Suspecting that he was plotting rebellion, Leo had him bound in the palace bath called the Pithekion, and ordered him to be tied to a pole and handed over to the fire of the furnace to be consumed; and the emperor himself stood watching him. But the empress Theodosia, with tearful entreaties, saved him from the bloodshed, and the emperor ordered the culprit to be let alone. To his wife he said: "Woman, today you have freed my soul from judgement in the next world, but perhaps you will soon deprive me of my life as well. You and our children will see what is going to happen." For the time of his death had been revealed to him from a certain book of counsel [?]. It contained a picture of this kind: the image of a lion, the whole beast, having on its head a Chi [?], and on its hindquarters a Phi [?], and in the middle of the beast, right at the loins, a sword, that is, a blade, stuck fast and bloodied. Showing this to Stephen, surnamed Kapetolites, he said to him: "What does this mean?" He answered: "Let it be, master; let me not even look at the picture." But Leo would not accept this. So Stephen, after reasoning it out, said to the emperor: "This lion stands for the person of the emperor, and between the letter Chi and the Phi some evil befalls him." And the emperor said: "What are the Phi and the Chi?" He said: "Between the Nativity of Christ and the feast of the Lights." There was also what had been told him through the patrician Bardanes by the monk living at Philomelion, and the matter of the putting on and handing over of the garments when he was entering the palace to take power. Besides this, his mother's vision filled him with fear. When it was told him at the time he had thought nothing of it, but now it pressed upon his soul and gnawed at it sorely. For while she was constantly visiting the divine church at Blachernae, there appeared to her a maiden surrounded by many people clothed in white, and the whole church was full of blood. This maiden told one of those standing by to fill a pot with blood and give it to Leo's mother to drink. When she pleaded her many years of abstinence, in which she had partaken neither of meat nor of anything with blood in it, and said that for this reason she had no need of this pot, the maiden retorted in anger: "And how is it that your son does not cease filling me with much blood and provoking this my Son and God?" From then on she often begged her son to depart from the heresy of the icon-burners, recounting the [?]

vision itself in tragic tones. Another vision by night terrified him no less than the first. He heard the celebrated patriarch Tarasios, who had long since departed this life, call a certain Michael by name; and Michael leapt forward, dealt the lion a mortal blow, and pushed it over a cliff above an abyss. 8. In the days of the godless Leo the Bulgarians came as far as the Gate, with no one meeting or hindering them. And Krum, performing a sacrifice according to his custom outside the Golden Gate, sacrificed men and many animals; and having wet his feet on the seashore and washed himself, and sprinkled his people and been acclaimed by them, he passed among his concubines, who bowed down to him and glorified him. All this he did while everyone looked on from the wall, and no one dared to hinder him or to loose an arrow at him. Having done everything he desired and wished, he encircled the city and threw up a palisade against it; and after spending some days and plundering the outskirts of the city, he began to demand a tribute [?] of gold, a great quantity of clothing, and a certain number of chosen girls [?]. So Leo, taking counsel with the officials, sent word to Krum: "Come down to the shore with a few men who carry no weapons, and we will come out by sea unarmed in a chelandion, and we will talk, and we will do all that you have asked." Having agreed on this, during the night they brought out three armed men and hid them in certain rooms of the [?] outside the Blachernae Gate, giving them a signal: "While we are conversing with Krum, we will make a certain sign; when you see it, come out and kill him." The next day, while the Bulgarians were near the Holy Anargyroi outside the city, Krum came down to the sea as agreed, with three others: his logothete; Constantine, called the son of Patzikos [?], who had fled to Bulgaria many years before; and Constantine's son, who was born of Krum's sister. These four [?] came down from among their people unarmed to the sea as agreed, not knowing of the ambush. Then the men from the city also came out in a chelandion, wishing to talk with Krum, and having received assurances they stepped off the vessel [?]. Krum dismounted and sat on the ground, and Constantine's son held his horse, saddled and bridled. And while they were conversing, one of the men from the city, Hexaboulios, gave the sign by uncovering his head with his hand. When Krum saw this,

he took alarm and leapt up; and since his horse was ready, those with him lifted him up and he mounted. And the people on the wall cried out: "The Cross has conquered!" And he began to flee. The armed men came out of the rooms and pursued Krum, and loosing their arrows they thought they had wounded him; but he escaped entirely alone to his people. The other three were seized by those in the chelandion. The logothete was slaughtered on the spot, while Constantine and his son were taken alive. 9. After these events Krum, enraged, ordered every place to be burned and laid waste the next day. They began burning and burned down all the churches across from the city, which were large and had been restored by Irene, Nikephoros and Michael; likewise the monasteries, the palaces, the houses and the suburbs. Coming to St Mamas, they burned the palaces there and the imperial bedchambers, broke the columns, carried off the lead and the statues of the hippodrome, and slaughtered all the captives, and the animals likewise. Passing along the coast of the Straits and the upper parts, they burned all the trading posts, and went off carrying much booty. Then, taking the right-hand side of the city toward the east [?], they burned everything outside the Golden Gate as far as Rhegion. Coming to Athyras, they destroyed the fortress there and the bridge, which was remarkable and very strong. Coming to Selymbria, they razed the fortress there to the ground and burned the churches and houses. After this they destroyed the fortress of Daonion. Coming to the city of Heraclea and being unable to get into it, they burned all the buildings at the harbour and around the city. After this, coming to Rhaidestos, they destroyed that fortress too, burning all the buildings and churches in it and slaughtering many people there. Coming to the fortress of Panion, they found it secured and holding many people; and being unable to do anything against it, they burned and destroyed everything outside and went up to Apros, which is also a fortress. Having destroyed and burned this too, and very many other fortresses, they went down from there over ten days and entered the mountains of Ganos. Finding there many people in hiding and almost all the livestock of Thrace, they slaughtered the people, and the animals, which were very numerous, they took as plunder and sent to Bulgaria, together with many women and children. Then they went off to Hexamilion and went down as far as Abydos, and turned back to the Hebros and the upper country, and destroyed all the fortresses, small and great, as far as Adrianople. Finding Adrianople strongly held, they laid siege to it. After spending many days and achieving nothing by the siege, they set up

[?] siege engines and assaulted the fortress. Then the besieged, hard pressed [?], having no help from anywhere and dying of hunger, surrendered. The Bulgarians took all the captives, who were countless in number, and all their goods, and resettled them in Bulgaria beyond the river Danube. While this was happening, Leo did not leave the city but held the empire tyrannically. When the feasts came round he crowned his son, who was small and named Symbatios, falsely saying that he was called Constantine. And gathering the people who had survived from the various cities, he gave them largesse and made them acclaim Leo and Constantine, imitating the former emperors Leo and Constantine the Isaurians, whose heresy he also revived, wishing to live many years as they had and to become famous. But God put his plan to shame and [?] his years. 10. Then, the weather in winter having turned fair and the rivers having little water, the Bulgarians came out thirty thousand strong, all clad in iron [?], and coming as far as Arkadioupolis and crossing the Rhegina (for that is what the river is called), they found many people and took them captive. Before they could take the captives across, there was heavy rain for eight days, and the river swelled and became like a sea. Unable to cross, the Bulgarians stayed fifteen days, holding the captives. When word was sent to Leo to come to the rescue, he paid no heed, nor did he leave the city or send anyone else to help. Then, when fair weather came and the river fell, they made the captives themselves cut wood and build a bridge, and so they crossed with the captives, men, women and children together, fifty thousand in all. They also took all their possessions, Armenian shaggy coverlets [?] and fine carpets [?] and much clothing and bronze vessels, loaded everything onto the wagons, and taking all their herds, cattle and sheep, they went into Bulgaria. And he who reigned unjustly by God's permission neither went out of the city himself to help the captives nor sent others. 11. After this it was reported to him that Krum had mustered a great army, gathering also the Avars and all the Sklaviniai; and that besides this he was preparing engines of various kinds of siege machines, devices and enormous catapults, triple-shot throwers [?] and stone-throwers, tortoises and tall ladders, balls and levers and borers [?], rams and arrow-stands, fire-throwers and stone-hurlers, and scorpions for shooting arrows, and

slings [?], all the engines to be used against the battlements to take the city. "It is against the western side of the city," it was said, "against the wall of Blachernae, that he means to bring up all these engines," where he had also been shot; and he was stabling ten thousand oxen to haul all the aforesaid machines, mounted on wagons, five thousand of which he had ordered to be bound with iron. When Leo heard this, he sent spies and learned the truth; then, gathering many people and craftsmen, he began to build another wall outside the wall of Blachernae, and also to dig a broad moat [?]. He had begun to build and had not yet finished when God, who scatters the counsels of nations, sets aside the reasonings of peoples and sets aside the counsels of rulers, showed that it is not by their own contrivance and strength that men can achieve anything. For when spring came, as some who escaped from captivity in Bulgaria report, around Holy Thursday of Easter the ruler of Bulgaria, Krum, the famous Krum who wished to take the city, came to the end of his life, slain by an invisible hand. Streams of blood poured from his mouth, his nostrils and his ears, and so he gave up his soul in misery. 12. Leo, then, puffed up in mind, as though he, and not God, had overthrown the enemy, sent imperial letters to all the provinces announcing: "Finding [?] the Bulgarians near the city, by my prudence and courage and my generalship I shot their ruler and destroyed them all; and that is why," he says, "our enemy dies." So much for this. 13. It is also said that a voice burst forth from heaven suddenly, announcing the good news of the overthrow of the godless emperor, and that it was heard by many at sea. They noted down the time and the hour (it was the tenth hour of the night), and later found it to be tr[ue]

14. Meanwhile Michael was held in prison and in chains. Since Leo intended to do away with him after the feast of Christ's Nativity, Michael sent word to his fellow conspirators, among whom was the keeper of the palace, saying: "If you do not hurry to get me out of custody, I will denounce you all to the emperor." They gathered together, put on phelonia as if they were priests, with swords carried underneath, and when the palace was opened and the emperor went into the church, they rushed in, hacked him limb from limb, and buried his body on the island of Prote. In that very hour they freed Michael from his chains and brought him in at the feast wearing a crown instead of chains. And the prophetic word was fulfilled: "Weeping will lodge in the evening, and in the morning there will be joy." His wife they had taken away to the monastery of the Despotai; and Symbatios [?]

his son, who had been renamed Constantine at his coronation, and the others, Basil and Gregory, together with [?], they tonsured on the island of Prote and made monks. There Constantine, renamed Basil, was struck dumb after his genitals were cut off, and he prayed to God, and also to Gregory the Theologian, whose image was set up there, that his voice might be loosed and his tongue recover its clear sound. And his prayer was heard. For at the festival of the Lights he saw that divine figure, which said: "Take the candle and read." Without hesitation he went in and read in a bright, clear voice: "Again my Jesus." From then on, abhorring the heresy handed down to him from his father, he honoured and embraced the images of the saints. But this happened later. Emperor of the Romans: Michael the Amorian, the Stammerer, the Iconoclast, 8 years, 9 months. 1. In the year of the world [?], the year of the divine Incarnation 814 [?], Michael the Amorian, the Stammerer and Iconoclast, became emperor of the Romans for 8 years and 9 months. He took as his wife Euphrosyne, the daughter of Constantine who had been blinded, though she had embraced the monastic life. He relaxed the earlier wickedness a little, so far that those in prison and exile had dreamlike glimpses of freedom and relief, but he cherished the God-hated mind of his impious predecessor; for, like [?], he was caught on the hook of the dreadful heresy out of utter irrationality and lack of education. So at a silention he said: "Those before us who examined the Church's ordinance of doctrines will give their own account for them, whether they decreed well or badly. In whatever state we found the Church proceeding, in that we choose to preserve it. Let honouring the icons and not honouring them be equally a matter of indifference." At this time the throne of the high priesthood was held by Antony, the son of Sylaios [?], who was hostile to the veneration of the holy icons. 2. After this Michael crowned Theophilos, his son by Euphrosyne, in the Great Church. Thomas the rebel set out from the eastern regions, dragging a rabble of mixed people along with him, and moved against Byzantium, aspiring to an empire he was unworthy of. He was a Roman of obscure origin who had gone to Syria, and renaming himself Constantine he claimed to be the son of the empress Irene. By this he deceived many barbarians and Romans, gathered a boundless multitude, and, boasting of his numbers, attacked Constantinople. He besieged it for three years, but when he saw his ships burned and the pick of his fighting men destroyed by the citizens, he was at a loss, left the city, and went into Thrace, plundering it. Michael went out of the city with a very large force and set out against
him; and having besieged him for a short time he subdued him without effort. He cut off his hands and feet and then impaled him, and so put an end to the civil war that had lasted three years.

3. While Michael was occupied with these matters, Crete, Sicily and the Cyclades islands were taken from the dominion of the Romans by Africans and Arabs, this loss then beginning for the first time because of the sins of the people and the impiety of the rulers. Such being the state of affairs, the emperor summoned Eirenaios the magistros and said to him: "I congratulate you, magistros: Sicily has rebelled." He replied: "This is no cause for joy, master." And turning to one of the great men he said: "A beginning of evils will fall upon the earth when a dragon rules over Babylon, utterly stammering of tongue and very fond of gold." 4. For the leader of the Hagarenes, Apochaps, put in at the cape of Crete and anchored at Charax, and ordered the people under him to leave their ships and plunder the country. When the army had gone off on this enterprise, he gave orders and burned their ships. When they grumbled about this, he said to them: "The other day you were grumbling at me, men, asking for land to settle in; that is why I have brought you here, where milk and honey flow." They answered him: "And where will we find our children and our wives?" He said to them: "You know that you have brought very many captives for yourselves; take wives for yourselves from among them." This pleased them, and they put a palisade around themselves as a fortification, from which the place is called Charax, "the palisade", to this day. Later a monk who came to the island said to them: "If you wish to master the island, follow me, and wherever I judge it best and show you a site suitable for building, build a city there, and through it you will gain control of the island." And he led them to a place called Chandax, where their city now stands, and they dug a moat around it. They took ninety cities and enslaved them; only one was not captured, but remained unbesieged by agreement, its inhabitants being allowed to practise the Christian faith freely. These are called tributaries to this day. And indeed the islands would have been subdued by the Hagarenes had not the emperor Michael commanded Krateros, the strategos of the Kibyrrhaiots, to make ready all the ships under him and sail to Crete. He arrived with two hundred ships and freed them; and sailing on to Crete he overcame all the Hagarenes there, and had resolved to put them to death, had not some of his people, ill-advisedly, prevented it, saying: "These men will never stand against us at night; let us seize them in the morning." And so, deceived,

…[?] at their words, still [?] to their tents [?] they returned, with no thought at all for their own safety. But the enemy fell on them in the night and brought an iron sleep on them all. Only their general got away, boarding a merchant ship and sailing off. When the leader of the Hagarenes learned of this, he put men aboard two transports and gave chase. He caught him off the island of Kos and impaled him there. Next, on the emperor's orders, the man surnamed Ooryphas gathered a naval levy. He gave each man forty gold pieces, and they boarded transports and sailed against Crete. They withdrew from the war having achieved nothing, and most of them were slaughtered there; the survivors were nicknamed the Forty-Piece Men. At this time the wonderworking bishop of Gortyna [?] of the island was slaughtered by the Hagarenes for Christ's sake, like a spotless sacrificial victim. His precious…

So it went with him. The impious Michael, however, fell gravely ill with strangury and pain in the kidneys, and he departed this life miserably. His wretched body was carried away and laid in the church of the Holy Apostles. Theophilus his son then held the empire together with his mother Euphrosyne. Emperor of the Romans: Theophilus the Iconoclast, son of Michael the Stammerer, 12 years. 1. Year of the world 6320 [?], year of the divine incarnation [?]. Emperor of the Romans [?]: Theophilus the son of Michael

the Stammerer, Iconoclast, 12 years. His mother Euphrosyne wished to give him a wife, so she brought in various maidens of incomparable beauty. Among them was one exceptionally lovely girl called Eikasia, and another named Theodora. His mother gave him a golden apple and told him to give it to the one who pleased him. The emperor Theophilus was struck by Eikasia's beauty and said, "So it was through a woman that evils flowed forth." She answered him, somewhat modestly, "But through a woman, too, the better things spring forth [?]." Her words wounded him to the heart. He let her be and gave the apple to Theodora, who came from Paphlagonia. The two of them were crowned by the patriarch Anthony in the oratory of Saint Stephen on holy Pentecost. From there he went to the Great Church, after lavishing a great deal of money on the patriarch and the clergy as well as the senate. Eikasia, having missed the throne, built a monastery. She took the veil there and lived a zealous life pleasing to God until her death, leaving many writings of her own. The emperor's mother Euphrosyne left the palace of her own accord and lived quietly in the monastery of Gastria. 2. When a horse race was held, the emperor had the chandelier brought out that had been cut through by a sword when Leo the Armenian was slain,

and he showed it to the whole senate in the imperial box. He said that the killers had dared to commit the murder inside a church of the Lord, but in truth he was angry because they had killed his fellow heretic, who shared his impious views. For the wretch held to that man's God-hated heresy. He pulled down some of the holy icons and dug out others, and he exiled and tortured monks for their piety. 3. In his second year Theophobus the Persian fled to the Romans together with his father and fourteen thousand Persians. The emperor distributed them among the themes, settling them there and organizing them into tourmai. Theophobus himself he made his brother-in-law by marrying him to the sister of Theodora Augusta, and this is how it came about. The Persians had a custom of proclaiming their king from the royal line. When the royal line died out in the successive wars, they were at a loss. They then learned that some members of the royal family had fled to the emperor of the Romans. For this reason they thought it desirable to leave their own country and go over to Roman territory for the sake of Theophobus, so that they might obtain a leader of their own race. This was all the more so because Babek, the leader of the Persians, had for five years been at the height of a revolt against the Amermoumnes. Wars broke out between the two, and Babek, defeated, entered Roman territory with seven thousand men. Searching [?] at the city of Sinope for the father of Theophobus, Babek seized him [?]. Then, having received guarantees from the emperor, he made himself and the people under him subjects of the emperor. Others, however, say that Theophobus' father came to Byzantium a poor man. He attached himself to a woman whose lot was to keep a tavern for hire, and, overcome by love for her, he lived with her for pleasure. She conceived by him and bore a male child. Now the Persians, who were expert in astronomy and divination, learned that a kinsman of the Persian king was living in Byzantium. So they came to the emperor and asked him to search for the one they had come for. The emperor heard this and made inquiries, but achieved nothing. Later they found the woman with whom the Persian Babek had lived. They learned that he had died, but that the boy born of their union was still alive, and they showed the boy to the emperor; he was twelve years old. The emperor took him and brought him up in the palace, and he enrolled the Persians in the military registers. 4. Now the emperor Theophilus, who loved splendor, built the Pentapyrgion from the ground up, along with the two great organs of solid gold set with various stones, and a golden tree on which perched birds that, by some

mechanism, sang musically, as air was sent in through hidden pipes. 5. He also renewed the imperial robes, the loroi and the rest, having them all made of cloth woven with gold. And he raised the city walls, which were low. He made a show of worldly justice, though he wronged the faith and true religion more than any emperor before him. Once at Blachernae, where he made a habit of going, a widow came up to him. She cried out that she was being wronged by the Augusta's brother Petronas, who was drungarios of the Watch. "He [?] his own buildings," she said, "and they block the light from mine and reduce them to nothing, since I am a despised widow." He immediately sent men to see whether this was true. When it was confirmed that the woman was telling the truth, he had the drungarios stripped in the middle of the street and severely beaten. He razed the buildings in question to the ground and gave the site to the widow. Another time a ship was passing by the Boukoleon. He asked whose it was and learned that it belonged to the empress. "Alas," he said, "I have been shown up as a shipowner, since this belongs to my wife." He sent men and burned the ship together with its cargo. 6. Theophilus' mother Euphrosyne was living as a nun in her own monastery of Gastria. It was her own house, which she had bought from the patrician Nicetas and turned into a convent for women, naming it Gastria. She would send for Theodora's daughters. There were five of them: Thecla, Anna, Anastasia, Maria and Pulcheria. She never stopped instructing them in all piety and in the discipline of the Lord, and in the veneration of the holy icons. This did not escape Theophilus. He called his daughters to him and questioned them about everything. The others, being right-minded, stoutly slipped out of his questions as if they were wrestlers' holds. But Pulcheria, still a baby in age and in mind, told him about the kindnesses and the quantities of fruit. Along with these she counted off the veneration of the holy icons as well. Without much thought, she said that there were lots of dollies in the chest, "and she puts them on our heads and faces after kissing them." This drove the emperor into a fury. Since he could do nothing to his mother, he simply cut off his daughters' visits to their grandmother. 7. Something similar happened to the empress Theodora as well. The emperor kept a deranged little man who differed in no way from Homer's Thersites (his name was Denderis). He babbled nonsense and made people laugh, and he lived in the palace for the sake of amusement. Once this fellow burst into the Augusta's bedchamber and found her holding holy icons and eagerly pressing them to her eyes. When the madman saw them, he asked what they were, and

came closer. She said, "My pretty dollies, like this, and I love them very much." The emperor happened to be dining at table just then, and when the fellow went straight to him, the emperor asked where he had been. He said he had been with "mama," meaning Theodora, and had seen her taking pretty dollies out from under her pillow. The emperor understood. Full of anger, he rose from the table and went straight [?] to her. He heaped many insults on her, calling her an idol-worshipper with his unbridled tongue, and at the same time he repeated [?] the madman's words. She, though for the moment she carried her anger in her breast, answered at once, "It is not that, O emperor, not what you supposed. I was looking into my mirror with my maidservants, and Denderis saw the figures appearing in it and foolishly went and reported it to his master and emperor." In this way she quenched his anger for the time being. A few days later she had Denderis punished and taught him to be sensible, telling him and instructing him never to say anything to anyone about the dollies. Once, at a drinking party, Theophilus, boasting and taunting his lady, asked him about her: was mama kissing the pretty dollies again? The madman put his right hand to his lips, grabbed his backside with his left, and replied, "Hush, hush about the dollies, O emperor!" 8. In his third year he married his daughter Maria to Alexios the Armenian, surnamed Mousele, a very brave and strong man, and made him a patrician and then a magistros. But he came to suspect that Alexios was aiming at the throne, so he sent him to Sicily as general and duke. And as envy will breed, some Sicilians came to the capital and slandered him to the emperor, saying, "He is betraying the Christians' interests to the Hagarenes and plotting against your reign." Meanwhile the emperor's daughter Maria died. The emperor adorned her coffin with silver and established a charter of freedom for any who took refuge at it. This silver the emperor Leo later removed. 9. In the same [?] year there was in the city, at the time Alexios was slandered, the archbishop Theodore, called Krithinos. The emperor gave him his own phylakterion and sent him to Sicily to give Alexios a pledge of safety and bring him back. When Alexios came, the emperor had him beaten as a rebel and put in prison, and confiscated all his property. Theodore was vexed and indignant when he learned of this. Shortly afterward, when the emperor went to Blachernae, Theodore went ahead of him and stood before the altar, clad in his priestly vestments. As the emperor approached the solea, he cried out in a loud voice: "Bend your bow, prosper, and reign! For what cause, O emperor?" The emperor, out of respect for the senate, replied: "For the sake of truth and meekness and righ-

teousness." Theodore said, "And what righteousness is there in you, when you gave Alexios a signed pledge through me and did not keep it?" The emperor, moved by uncontrollable rage, dragged him away from the altar by force, had him severely beaten, and sent him into exile. He did this not only because he had been rebuked by him, but also because he had learned that Theodore revered and honored the holy icons and denounced his own impiety. Not long afterward, when the emperor came to the Great Church, the patriarch reproached him, and he brought the archbishop back with apologies. Theodore judged himself unworthy of the priesthood because of what he had suffered, so the emperor made him steward of the Great Church. He also released Alexios from prison, restored all his property to him, and held him in honor. Alexios became a monk and built the monastery of Anthemios. He died there and was given a holy burial. 10. In his fifth year Manuel, the most famous general of the whole East, was held in great honor by the emperor. Once, after exchanging some words with Myron, logothete of the dromos and father-in-law of Petronas, he was slandered to the emperor as aiming at the throne, and terrible things were being plotted against him. But Leo the protovestiarios, who looked after Manuel and protected him, kept assuring the emperor that what was said against him was false. When Manuel learned of this, he slipped away from the emperor's anger and the slanders. He left the city secretly, went as far as Pylai, and mounting the public post horses fled to the passes of Syria, hamstringing the horses as he went. He sent word to the Hagarenes: "I am fleeing the emperor's wrath. If you will not force me to abandon my faith, I take refuge with you. If you will receive me on these terms, send me a pledge of safety." They gladly sent the pledge and received him as if he were emperor of the Romans. When the emperor heard this he fell into great distress and despondency, and he took counsel about it with John the synkellos. John said: "If you earnestly want Manuel to come back to you, O emperor, I myself am ready to bring it about. Let me take money and be sent to the Amermoumnes, supposedly to visit those held in prison and in chains, carrying a signed pledge from your majesty to persuade Manuel to come and meet me. I expect to succeed through the signed pledge, through my powers of persuasion, through his piety, and because he very likely still loves his homeland." The emperor gave him a great deal of money and gifts and sent him off. John went in, distributed largesse to the prisoners, and won over the chief counselor. In this way he managed to meet Manuel secretly and give him the signed pledge and the emperor's phylakterion. With this done, he returned and reported everything to the emperor. Manuel then made a request of the Amermoumnes concerning the Roman captives held in prison, giving him his word on their behalf

that they would not run away if they were let out, but would fight hard. His request was granted. Taking the son of the Amermoumnes and a large army, he set out against the Persians and won a great victory. He also freed the Hagarenes from the Theroi [?], who were ravaging them. As a result he was held in even greater honor than before, and he became all-powerful with the Amermoumnes. But he was very anxious to get away to Romania, and after some time he said to the potentates of Syria, "If you give me the son of the Amermoumnes and an army and let me set out, I can subdue Romania." They told the Amermoumnes, and he was sent. Manuel came near the themes of the East. He called together those under his command, and also the son of the Amermoumnes, supposedly to exercise and to hunt. When they were far from the enemy, he embraced and kissed the son of the Amermoumnes and said: "I am going to the emperor and to my own people, for I have valued nothing in life above my faith and my kin. As for you, go back with your men to your own people, and fear no harm from us." The young man went back in tears and in shame, while Manuel went on to the emperor, sending a messenger ahead to announce his coming. The emperor rewarded the messenger generously and received Manuel as was fitting. He at once made him magistros and domestic of the Schools, and he stood sponsor to his children at holy baptism. 11. In his seventh year the emperor set out against the Hagarenes with Manuel, the senate and the whole army. He easily took Zapetra and Samosata, which was rich in wealth because the Amermoumnes came from there, and he returned exulting in his victory and his spoils. When he reached Bryas he ordered a palace to be built there, parks to be planted, and water to be brought in, and all this was done. Then he came to the city and held a horse race. He drove the first heat himself in a white chariot, paraded the spoils in triumph, and was crowned, while the factions acclaimed him: "Welcome, incomparable factionarius!" 12. In his eighth year the patriarch Anthony died, and in his place John the synkellos was ordained. He was better called Jannes and Jambres: the grammarian mentioned under Leo the Armenian and apostate, notorious for sorcery, divination by bowls and every kind of impiety. He proved a fit instrument for the emperor's impiety and worked with him at everything that led to ruin. The basilisk of impiety that the emperor had been carrying in his womb and holding back he now brought to birth, bursting forth with it [?]: he ordered the holy icons to be smeared over or painted out.

13. This John built a house of dressed stone outside the city, which to this day is called the Troulos. There, by means of certain sacrifices, he consorted with demons and revealed the future to the emperor. Because of the demonic visitations that took place there at that time, the house remained uninhabited. 14. Meanwhile the emperor learned that a certain Hagarene woman, whom he had taken captive and who had a spirit of divination, could prophesy. He sent for her and asked her whose dynasty would last for many years. She answered, "That of the Martinakioi." Convinced by this pretext, he condemned Martinakios to the monastic life and turned his house into a monastery for monks. She also foretold to Constantine Triphyllios what would happen to him: "You and your children will likewise be tonsured as clerics under the emperor Basil," and this came to pass. In the same way she foretold to many others what would happen to them. She foretold precisely to the emperor what was to happen after his death, including the veneration of the icons and the deposition of Jannes. And she told George, who was in charge of the military registers, that he would be killed at the Sphendone of the hippodrome and that his property would be taken into the imperial treasury. 15. In his ninth year the Arabs marched out against Romania in great force. The emperor went against them with the Persian refugees, the tagmata and Manuel the domestic. Battle was joined and the emperor was defeated. He went into the midst of the Persians, supposing that they would save him. Looking around, Manuel saw that the emperor was among the Persians, and that they were already intending to hand him over to the Arabs and so make their peace with them. He cut his way through them, seized the bridle of the emperor's horse and dragged him out against his will. He thought it an unbearable disgrace if the Arabs should take the emperor of the Romans captive. But the emperor, beside himself with fear at the situation, wanted to rejoin the Persians. Manuel raised his sword as if to strike him, and in fear he came away. From there he returned in disgrace to Dorylaion. Manuel had been wounded in the battle. He fell ill and died, after performing many brave deeds against the Hagarenes. His body was carried to the monastery he had built, which lies near the cistern of Aspar. 16. At once there were slanders to the emperor against the Persians, and threats against Theophobus as a rebel, a traitor and an enemy. When Theophobus learned of this, he took the Persians and went down as far as Sinope. Sinope took its name from one of the Amazons, who founded it. Amastris, formerly called Kromna, was named after Amastris the Persian, daughter of Oxyartes the brother of Darius. She married Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea, and the city, being under him,

…had named the city after his wife. Having taken it, he held it as a tyrant. When the emperor learned of this he was deeply grieved. Fearing that they might go over to the Arabs, he went as far as Paphlagonia. He gave them assurances that they would suffer no harm, took Theophobos with him and returned to the City, while the other Persians went back to wherever each had first been settled. Theophobos was loved by the citizens no less than by the Persians, as an orthodox man.

17. In his tenth year a son was born to the emperor by Theodora, and he named him Michael. As the emperor was going to Blachernae, as was the custom, a man met him and said, "The horse your majesty is riding is mine." He asked, "Who is it that [?]?" The man said, "The count of the Opsikion sent it to your majesty." The next day the emperor summoned the count of the Opsikion, who happened to be in the City, and said, "Whose is the horse?" He said, "I bought it." When the complainant contradicted him and said that he had taken it by force and without paying, the emperor said, "Why did you not take the price beforehand?" He answered, "I was offering him a hundred nomismata. But he wanted to become a scholarios, and when he failed in that because he was a coward, he would not even take the hundred nomismata." Satisfied by this that the horse had been taken by force, the emperor gave it back, and ordered that the man also be made a scholarios. But he did not want to take the horse; he received two pounds of gold and went away.

18. When the Saracens came against Amorion, the emperor marched out swiftly as far as Cappadocia. The Amermoumnes set apart an army of fifty thousand, gave them Goundees as commander, a man most renowned among the Hagarenes, and sent them against the emperor. Battle was joined; the emperor was defeated and fled, and returned in disgrace, barely escaping with his life. The Saracens threw a palisade around Amorion and fought many engagements, but when they saw that those inside were fighting steadfastly they wanted to withdraw. Then a disciple of Leo the Philosopher who was in the fortress sent them word: "If you hold out for two days, you will take us." And so it happened, for the city was betrayed by the man called Boiditzes and by Manikophanes. Among the faithful, men of the greatest renown were captured: the patrikios Theophilos; the generals Melissenos and Aetios; the protospatharios Theodore and the eunuch Krateros; Kallistos the tourmarch; Constantine the droungarios; Bassoes the Runner; and some officers of the tagmata. Wishing to ransom them, the emperor sent envoys to the Amermoumnes with two hundred kentenaria. But he could not persuade him. The Amermoumnes said, "Even if you give me a thousand kentenaria for the army I have assembled, I will not set a single one of them free."

19. So the captives were led away to Syria, and they were much [?] by the protosymboulos

[?], and indeed by Boiditzes as well, through seven years of imprisonment. They would not be persuaded to deny Christ, and they were beheaded with the sword, loving eternal life rather than this passing one. After one day they were thrown into the river. Most wonderful of all, each head, after it had been cut off, was joined and grew together again with its own body. And just as their souls are in one place in paradise, so the bodies of the saints were given one and the same reverence by the faithful. When they had been martyred, the protosymboulos ordered that Boiditzes too be beheaded, saying, "If this man were a true Christian, he would not have betrayed [?] his own." This was done, and his body was thrown out together with the saints, but it was found lying outside their row. His head was far from his body, not joined to it like those of the saints. When they were thrown into the river, the crowd watched all the bodies of the saints float safely across to the far bank, while his body alone the crocodiles dragged about, tore apart and devoured.

20. The disciple of Leo the Philosopher, who had given word of the betrayal, was questioned by the Amermoumnes about his learning, and said that he was a disciple of Leo the Philosopher. When the Amermoumnes learned what sort of man Leo was, he longed to see him. He gave letters for Leo the Philosopher to one of the captives and sent him to Constantinople, promising Leo that he would be second only to himself in honour. Leo received the letters and took them to the emperor Theophilos. When the emperor learned of the man's learning, and that he had so wise a man in his own city, he brought him into the palace and installed him in the Magnaura. He also gave him pupils to teach, the most gifted of the young, and freed him from every care. This man afterwards became metropolitan of Thessalonica as well, ordained by the most holy patriarch Methodios.

21. In his eleventh year the emperor built in the palace the Triconch, the so-called Sigma and the stands of the demes. He also set up the Phiale, where the so-called saximodeximon takes place, with the horses of both factions passing by in golden trappings. Beneath the Triconch, by an ingenious device, he made the so-called Mysterion, in which whatever someone says in secret, bending close into one corner, is clearly heard in the other.

22. Meanwhile the emperor Theophilos learned that Theophanes, the composer of church canons and hymns, and his brother Theodore, who lived on their own, were mocking his impiety and refuting it. He had them brought to him and said, "Where are you from?" They said, "From Palestine." Theophilos said, "And why, when you have left your own land and come to ours, do you not obey my majesty?" When they made no answer, [?]

he ordered that they be struck hard in the face. Then, after having them flogged with ox-sinews almost to the point of death, he said angrily to the eparch, "Take them to the praetorium, make up some verses and tattoo [?] them on their faces. And if the verses are not good, do not let that trouble you." He said this because the holy men were very learned. The saints said, "Write, emperor, write what you please, since you will have to read it out before the just Judge." The eparch took the saints to the praetorium and inscribed these verses not only on their faces but also on their chests:

While all men long to hasten to the city
Where once the all-pure feet of God the Word
Stood firm to bring salvation to the world,
These wicked vessels of a superstitious error
Wrought many shameful deeds there through unbelief,
Dreadful deeds, with an impious mind,
And so were driven out from there as apostates.
They fled to the City of the empire,
Yet did not give up their lawless follies.
Therefore, branded on their faces as evildoers,
They are condemned and driven out once more.

After this inscription he sent them into exile. As they were travelling with the public post-horses, they happened to stop at Karta Limen. Now the great Methodios had been shut up by that hater of God, Theophilos, in a tomb on the island of Antigonos with two robbers. So Theodore and Theophanes wrote to him through a most faithful fisherman, who also served the holy Methodios in his humble needs. Because of the darkness of the tomb he had brought him a lamp, and every Saturday he brought him a follis' worth of oil, which was enough to give light to the prisoners for the seven days. Once it happened that the fisherman fell ill and did not bring the usual Saturday supply. But at the saint's prayer God made up the lack, and the lamp, which was about to go out, kept shining until the following Saturday. It was through this fisherman, then, that they wrote:

To the living dead man and the life-giving corpse,
Who dwells upon the earth and walks the heavens,
The inscribed prisoners write to the prisoner.

The saint replied to them through the same fisherman:

To those whose names are written in the books of heaven,
Who on their foreheads have been branded for their virtue,
The one buried alive sends greeting, as to fellow prisoners.

23. Theodore, now among the saints, died in exile. His relics were later brought by Michael, the founder himself, to the monastery of Michaelitzes in Chalcedon. The celebrated Theophanes lived on into the reign of Michael and Theodora, and was ordained metropolitan of Nicaea by Methodios, now among the saints, once he had become patriarch. When some were displeased at his ordination and said, "He is a Syrian, and who knows whether he is orthodox?", since no one had testified for him, the holy Methodios answered, "Better

than this testimony that he bears" (and he pointed to the writing on his face) "I want none."

24. It is worth telling, too, how the holy Methodios was recalled from the tomb. For seven years he had been shut up with two robbers in a most dreadful and narrow tomb. Theophilos had condemned him to this, together with unbearable beatings, the breaking of his jaws and the tearing out of his teeth, because he venerated the holy icons. The tomb had only one small hole, through which he received his meagre food and water. In the second year one of the robbers happened to die there. You know well what stench arises, and how worms devour the body, once the soul has left it. Yet the noble men, the holy Methodios and the robber who was left, endured this hardship. When the seven years were over, the saint was brought out of the tomb in the following way. The emperor Theophilos, who devoted his leisure to study, found in the palace library, by God's providence, a piece of writing that he could not understand. He sent it to the patriarch John, and likewise to Leo the Philosopher, who, as was said above, taught philosophy in the Magnaura. Both of them failed. The emperor was distressed and vexed about it, and for some days went about downcast and without eating. Then one of the koubikoularioi took courage and said to the emperor, "My lord, no one else can explain this writing except Methodios, who is shut up in the tomb. If your majesty commands, I will take what you want answered and go to him by night, as though without your majesty's knowledge, and you will surely receive a clear interpretation of it." The emperor agreed. When the koubikoularios went to the island, while he was still far off he heard the saint saying, "Welcome, brother John the koubikoularios" (for that was his name). "I know why you have come, sent by Theophilos. But give me paper and ink." He took them and set out the answer in three solutions. When Theophilos read them he was astonished. He sent and brought Methodios to the palace and lodged him near himself in the so-called Sigma, ordering that no one from outside should go in to him except the man who served Theophilos. The emperor himself went in to him every day and inquired into the questions he wanted answered. The robber who had been left there, though he was set free, refused to come out, and died there, honoured with great signs and wonders.

25. At this same time the golden finial of the lantern in the Augusteion of Justinian fell down, and the emperor gave the steeplejack a hundred nomismata. Theophilos crowned his son Michael in the Great Church, lavishing gifts on everyone, as was the custom, in the

…hospice now called that of Theophilos. It had originally been the house of the patrikios Isidore, who came up from Rome with Olybrius in the time of Constantine. Some years later it was assigned as a curatoria, for women of [?] to live in. Under Leo the Isaurian it was turned by him from a brothel into a hostel. Then it became the house of Constantine, the son of Irene, after his mother had had him blinded. When he died, his wife became a nun, turned it into a monastery and called it ta Metanoias. Now a very large beam of the triclinium broke and threatened to fall, and as the emperor was passing by, the nuns petitioned him about it. He turned aside, looked over the house and liked it. So he moved the nuns to another monastery, adorned the house with every kind of decoration and made it a hospice, endowing it with money and estates and naming it ta Theophilou.

27. The emperor was stricken with dysentery, and took counsel with those who shared his views about Theophobos the Persian. He knew that the Persians, and not a few of the officials as well, had great trust in him and love for him, and he feared that after his own death they might make him emperor and push aside his son Michael. So he sent and had him brought to the palace and kept him under guard. Then, weighed down by his illness, he ordered him to be beheaded. When he saw the head he said, "Now, Theophobos, you have found rest, and I am free of worry." And at once he breathed out his spirit, wretchedly and in pain. His body was carried to the church of the Holy Apostles, and that of Theophobos to his own house near ta Narsou. When the Persians then asked after Theophobos and what had become of him, the emperor's people persuaded them that he was living in the palace. This is how the story spread among the Persians, down to our own times, that Theophobos never tasted death.

Michael and Theodora, Emperors of the Romans

1. In the year of the world 6335, the year of the divine Incarnation 835, Michael and Theodora reigned as emperors of the Romans for fourteen years; Michael alone for twelve years, and with Basil for one year and four months; altogether twenty-seven years and four months. Theodora, who was pious, faithful and orthodox, had honoured and venerated the holy icons in secret while her husband was still alive. By her own decision, but at the suggestion and urging of Theoktistos, the kanikleios and logothete, she drove the godless patriarch John out of the Church, even though he was her co-godparent, and confined him in a monastery at the Stenon, in the place called Kleidion. When he gouged the eyes of the icons of Christ our God, of the Mother of God and of the archangels there, she wanted to have his own eyes put out; but being prevented by [?], she sent and had him flogged with two hundred lashes. And she

installed Methodios, now among the saints, as patriarch. She brought back together the monks and bishops whom Theophilos had exiled, confirmed the orthodox faith and gave the Church peace on the first Sunday of Lent.

This is how Theodora drove the wicked Iannes out of the patriarchate. She sent him word through Constantine, the droungarios of the Watch: "Many pious men and monks, who have gathered from many places, have petitioned my majesty to order that the venerable icons be set up again. If, then, you agree with them and are of one mind with them, let the Church of God recover its ancient adornment. But if you are in doubt and your mind is not right, leave the throne and the City and withdraw to your suburban estate, until a council of the holy fathers can meet with you. For they are ready to go to judgment and debate with you, and to prove that you are wrong about these matters." The patriarch, or rather the faction-leader, was at that moment reclining on a couch in the Thessalian triclinium of the patriarchate, receiving the imperial messages. As soon as he heard the words he was struck to the heart. He said he would consider the matter carefully and promptly sent the messenger away. Then, quicker than it takes to tell, he took a small knife and cut the veins of his belly. He knew that the copious flow of blood would stir fear and pity in the crowd, but would bring no death or danger at all. At once a murmur and an outcry spread around the Church, and it reached the imperial ears even before the droungarios did, that the empress had had the patriarch murdered through the droungarios. The patrikios Bardas was sent to investigate the report thoroughly. He quietly established that the wounds had been made deliberately, and the play-acting did not escape exposure: the servants themselves denounced it to him, and the instruments of the cutting, which were lancets, were brought out for all to see. From then on he was not given any hearing, since he had been caught in so flagrant an offence. The wretch was driven from the Church and confined in a monastery at Kleidion. There, when he [?] the icons of the saints, the empress punished him with two hundred lashes, and in his suburban estate [?]

2. Now this John, the patriarch mentioned above, whom the pious called Iannes because of his impiety, was no incomer or foreigner. He was a native, a scion of the queen of cities, descended from a very noble lineage, the one called that of the Morocharzanioi. He had formerly been hegoumen of the monastery of the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus in ta Hormisdou, and was counted among the emperor's clergy. He was especially loved by Michael the Stammerer, whether simply because he shared his heresy, or also because he [?]

had gained some reputation for excelling in learning. In any case he was loved, and was appointed tutor to Theophilos. When Theophilos took the reins of empire, he first honoured him with the rank of synkellos and later made him patriarch of Constantinople, because John announced to him certain things in advance through lecanomancy and sorcery. The sorcery was of this kind. Once a nation, faithless and harsh, led by three commanders, was overrunning and plundering the land of the Romans. Theophilos and all his subjects were naturally disheartened at this. John advised him to put away his despondency and be filled with courage and joy, if only he would follow his counsel. And his counsel was this. Among the bronze statues on the Euripos of the Hippodrome, there was said to be a statue formed with three heads, which by some talismanic enchantment he linked to the leaders of that nation. He ordered three huge iron hammers to be made and put into the hands of three very strong men. Late at night they went to the statue together, Iannes disguised in lay clothing and the men holding the hammers raised. He pronounced the words of the enchantment and told each of them to strike with all his might, vigorously and hard. Two of them knocked off two of the statue's heads; the third only bent his head a little, and did not sever it completely from the body. What happened to the leaders followed this pattern. A fierce quarrel broke out among them and civil war, and two of the leaders fell at the hands of the third, just as the heads had been cut off; only the third survived, and he not unharmed. So the nation, reduced to nothing, set off home again in flight and disaster.

3. When Theodora, beloved of God as was said, had given the Church back its adornment (for from Leo the Amalekite until the restoration of orthodoxy the icon-burners had held the churches for thirty years), she made a request of the holy fathers who were present, saying, "I know that God has given you authority on earth to forgive sins, according to the Gospel of Christ. Now the emperor Theophilos, as you all know, was a just judge if anyone ever was, and governed everything well, as you yourselves testify. He held only this one heresy, and he renounced it as he was dying: with tears, at the very hour of his departure, when I handed him the holy icons, he kissed them, and so breathed his last. So grant me this favour yourselves: that this one sin be forgiven him, in writing. About the rest I have no concern." At first the fathers were silent. Then they wept, moved by her tears; and since they also sought honour for the holy icons, by common vote and agreement they gave the empress an assurance of this in a written guarantee. After this the church [?]

[?] having arrived, and having restored to the most holy Methodius the honour of the high priesthood, on the first Sunday of the holy fasts they and the empress kept an all-night service of hymns, from evening onward, in the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae. At dawn they went in procession to the great sanctuary of the Word of God, and the Church once more received its proper adornment. The divine liturgy was celebrated in purity, and all the heretics everywhere under the sun were deposed, together with their high priest, who was the John mentioned above. 4. This man, then, deposed together with his gang, as has been said, did not choose to live out his despicable life in quiet, but still kept up his insolence against the holy icons. Exiled again to a certain monastery, where a holy icon stood on the ceiling and gazed steadily down at him, he could not bear to see its gaze coming down upon him.
