He ordered a servant to take it down and gouge out its eyes, saying only this: "I cannot look upon its face." When the empress heard of this, she had the eyes of that Jannes himself put out. But even so he would not be content to love quiet. With those of his kind he tried to fasten some disgrace on Methodius, now among the saints: they talked a certain woman round and brought against him a charge of secret fornication. But the most blessed patriarch, not wishing to be counted a stone of stumbling, uncovered his private parts, and they were found to be withered beyond what was natural. Asked the cause, he said: "While I was living in Rome, since I was troubled by the titillations of desire, I went to the apostle Peter in prayer. He appeared to me at night, gripped my members with his right hand, and declared that henceforth I need not fear the lust of pleasure. I woke in severe pain, and from then on I remained unharmed." Moreover the woman, held securely, told everything, and she showed the gold that had been given to her, still wrapped in its bundles and sealed with their seal. They wished to punish the men, but at the entreaty of the holy Methodius they let them go. 5. At this feast, then, the one called the Sunday of Orthodoxy, the empress Theodora entertained the whole body of the Church in the palace of Karianos. Theophilos had built it for his daughters, though it had first been put up by the emperor Maurice. There was not one of the priests and confessors who was not present there, and among them was Theophanes of Nicaea. When the feasting was over and the sweetmeats and cakes were set out, the empress kept gazing at the letters on the forehead of the holy Theophanes and sighing. And it happened that he too, as if by agreement, saw her with his own eyes and noticed her staring at him. So he said, "What, then, is the reason for your [?]

intent gaze at me?" She said she marvelled at the endurance he had shown under the lettering, and at the cruelty of the man who had done it. The blessed Theophanes, with no caution and no thought for the assurances given earlier, said very plainly: "For this writing I will contend fiercely with your husband before God's impartial tribunal." Hearing this, the empress was deeply grieved and in tears, and said to the holy man: "Are these your written promises and professions, that not only have you not forgiven him, but you will even bring him to trial?" "No," said the patriarch, rising at once, and so did the rest of the priests, "no, empress. Our commitments will surely stand, and this man's carelessness counts for nothing." So the matter was hushed up, and the customs of the Church [were kept] untroubled. 6. There also appeared another heresy, called that of the Zelikes, with its own founder, who was named Zelix and held the first rank among the imperial secretaries. He was healed and brought over to true religion in an imperial procession. Those who adhered to the heresy were judged worthy of anointing with chrism alone, together with new baptismal robes and garments, and were splendidly initiated. 7. In her second year Theodora sent Theoktistos the logothete against Crete. He handled his men badly, and while he himself took to flight, the army became work for the swords of those in Crete. 8. In her third year, when Amer campaigned against the Romans, Theodora again sent him with a large force. A battle took place at Mauropotamos, and once more he was defeated: many were killed, and still more were taken captive. Theoktistos, however, came to the empress and kept his intimacy with her. Falling into words with Bardas, the brother of the Augusta Theodora, he laid the defeat on him and blamed him, claiming that it was by his advice and counsel that the Roman army had been mauled. 9. In the seventh year, when the emperor Michael had come to manhood and was giving himself up to hunting and impurity, Theodora learned that he had become intimate with Eudokia, the daughter of Inger, a woman hated by the Augusta and the logothete for her shamelessness. So she married him to Eudokia, the daughter of Dekapolites, and they were crowned in the church of Saint Stephen in the Daphne. 10. In his tenth year the strategos of the Boukellarioi brought the emperor a marvellous and noble horse. It was so very wild that no one could even look at its teeth to tell its age. The emperor was vexed at this, and Theophilitzes, who was then count of the Noumera and of the Walls, being present, said to the emperor: "I have a young man, very skilled and bold with horses, just such as your majesty likes, named Basil." At the emperor's command he was brought at once, and with one hand

he seized the horse by the ear and changed it into something as tame as a sheep. The emperor was delighted at this and handed him over to Andrew the hetaireiarch, to be enrolled in the Hetaireia and to serve the emperor's horses. 11. This Basil came from Macedonia, from the villages around Adrianople. He had attached himself to Tzantzes, the strategos of Macedonia, as his servant, and was then twenty-five years old. Having gained nothing from him, he came to the City. He entered within the Golden Gate, and since he was worn out from the journey, it being Sunday evening, he lay down on the bench at the church of Saint Diomedes, which had formerly been a church of Elijah. It was a parish church, under a warden named Nicholas. That night someone appeared to Nicholas and called out: "Get up and bring the emperor inside." He got up, but found no one except Basil lying there like a beggar, so he turned back and lay down again on his bed. The same thing happened a second time. The third time the figure struck him in the side with a sword, saying: "Do you not see the man lying outside the gate? He is the emperor. Bring him in." So he hurried out, trembling, found Basil with his bag and staff, and brought him in. The next day he bathed him, gave him a change of clothes, made him his sworn brother, and made merry with him. Nicholas had a brother, a physician in the service of the Theophilitzes mentioned above. He happened to come to his brother Nicholas and saw Basil, and marvelling at his stature and appearance he asked his brother where he came from. Nicholas told him everything except the vision. A few days later, when Theophilitzes was looking for a bold man for his horses, the physician was present and told him about Basil. Basil was quickly brought, and when Theophilitzes saw him he was delighted with him. Since he was [?] and large-headed, he called him Kephalas, and gave him his horses to look after. From there, as has been said, he was given to the emperor Michael. The emperor Michael brought Basil to his mother and said: "Come and look, mother, at a man I have just acquired." She came out, saw him, and turned away, saying: "This, my child, is the one who will wipe out our family." But the emperor was not persuaded at all, and paid no heed to his mother. 12. In his eleventh year Methodius, the patriarch now among the saints, died, and in his place Ignatius was ordained, the son of the kouropalates who had been emperor. When the Bulgarians were plundering Thrace and Macedonia, Theodora sent [?] and checked their onslaught.

13. In his thirteenth year Bardas, later the Caesar, who was living outside the City, became friends with Damian, patrikios and parakoimomenos. Damian had the emperor's ear and persuaded him to let Bardas come into the City and to the palace. Bardas also won over the protospatharios Theophanes Phalganes and certain others, and killed Theoktistos in the palace, with the emperor's knowledge. When Theodora learned this, she was indignant against the emperor and the others who had carried out the murder, and cried out against them. But terrified by a harsh voice, she withdrew to her chamber lamenting. For one of the retired generals, whose family descended from the Melissenoi, told her to run back home, calling such a day one of [?]. Michael tried every means to appease his mother, but she remained inconsolable. So the emperor changed: as his soul and mind changed, so did his bearing and his conduct, and he set about grieving her in as many ways as he had before pretended to serve her. He moved his sisters Thekla, Anastasia and Anna to the Karianos, but Pulcheria, as her mother's favourite, to the monastery of Gastria. Then shortly afterwards he gathered them all together in the monastery of Gastria and had them tonsured. At that time he was proclaimed by the whole senate and ruled as sole emperor, and he promoted Bardas to [?] and domestic of the Schools. His mother grieved at this [?], and also because of the unjust slaughter of Theoktistos, so that there was implacable enmity between them. He therefore sent her too down to Gastria. There, her mind drowned in despondency and her good sense taken from her by shock, she devised a plot against Bardas unworthy of herself. She took as her partners many others, among them the emperor's protostrator, intending to kill Bardas as he returned from his suburban estate at Kosmidion. But the plan came to light before the deed, and the evil fell on the very men who had planned it: they were found out, condemned, and beheaded in the Sphendone. Michael then promoted Basil in place of the dead protostrator, and likewise his uncle Bardas to kouropalates. 14. In his second year [?] dust fell from heaven, full and blood-coloured, and many people found stones as red as blood. Michael gave himself over to every vice and squandered the money in the palace, which amounted to more than one thousand and ninety centenaria of gold, besides a countless quantity of silver, all of which his mother had stored up. He stood godfather at holy baptism to the children of the charioteers, and gave each of them a hundred nomismata, or fifty at the least. And there was once a patrikios, called Himerios the Pig, a name he got from the fierceness of his face. He was talking obscenely at table, and let out a noise from his profane belly in the face of the

emperor and his fellow diners, so loud that, by an extraordinary marvel, the little lamp lighting them was blown out by the blast. To this man Michael gave a hundred gold nomismata. 15. In this way he wasted the public funds on nothing that was needed. Before even a single season had gone by, the time came for the soldiers' pay and there was no source of money. So he melted down that golden and much-celebrated plane tree, the two lions and the two griffins, all of solid hammered gold, the organ of solid gold, and other works besides weighing [?] two hundred centenaria, together with eight hundred robes of solid gold and gold thread. He had it struck into coin and paid the soldiers' wages. When Basil came to power, he found nothing but thirteen centenaria and [?] miliaresia. At a loss, he ordered the coin now called the senzaton to be struck, and took care of the treasury. 16. To confirm what I have said by recounting a little more, and to make plainer the boorishness and folly of the man, if indeed one ought to call him a man: he was standing in a chariot, about to spring from the starting gate, when news arrived that Amer was ravaging the Thrakesion terribly and, having made his way into the Opsikion, was approaching the Malagina, and that horrors such as had never yet been seen were expected. At this the protonotarios was downcast and reported with dejection the reply from the domestic of the Schools, holding the letters in his hands and showing them. But Michael said: "You there, how dare you try to talk about such things during this crucial race of mine? All I care about is not to see the middle left horse turned round, and on that my whole [?] depends." 17. But I will tell another thing of his, worse than this one, which not only falls short of what is fitting but is utterly foreign to imperial dignity. He met a certain woman whose child he had sponsored at baptism, as she was coming from the bath carrying her jar in her hands. He got down from his horse and sent the rest of his company to the palace. Then, taking along some debauched and secret little fellows, he went off with the woman, having taken the jar from her hands. "Come now, woman, don't be afraid," he said. "Have me at your house. I have a craving for bran bread and soft cheese." No doubt he supposed that, out of the fifty nomismata he had given her husband, she had acquired something. The woman was dumbfounded at this strange sight, since she was short of everything. Michael himself laid her bath towel, still soaking wet, on the bench in place of a tablecloth, for she had no table. He took her key from her, and the emperor was everything at once: table-setter, cook and guest. Bringing out what that poor woman's chest held, he feasted [Notes: 'ἐχόντων' P; 'τὰ' omitted in P; for 'μυστικὰ' (secret), Scylitzes has 'πορνικά' (lewd).]

with her and dined with her, and from there he strolled back again to the palace. 18. And what was worse: the band of those he kept with him were satyr-like men, unrestrained in every obscenity, and he held them in honour and respect while he despised divine things. He dressed them in gold-woven priestly vestments and omophoria, and made them perform the holy rites shamefully and impurely. Their leader, named Gryllos, he called patriarch, and the other eleven he called metropolitans of the chief and most illustrious sees. Unless he took part with them himself, he did not think himself fit to reign. The bishop of Koloneia, as they styled one of them, held the first throne, and the twelfth was the emperor Michael himself. They sang the hymns to the cithara, mimicking the secret prayers with shrill strumming and the exclamations with unrestrained and piercing force. They had vessels gilded and set with pearls, which they filled with vinegar and mustard and gave to whomever they wished to make communicants, mocking in this way the immaculate mysteries. This Gryllos also rode on a white she-ass, making public processions, and delighted in having such a troupe following him. And once it happened that he met the blessed Ignatius as he was coming with a church procession. Hitching up his phelonion, he and his fellow initiates began to strum more loudly, and he showered the clergy with countless most shameful words. Rebuked by the holy man, he paid no heed to any of it, but for the moment he turned off the road. By these things that most senseless man made himself an object of indecent laughter and guffaws, and through them the holy offering was outraged, and the holy words were outraged, being recited and chanted over their unspeakable and impure practices. 19. Not long afterwards the most holy Ignatius was brought down from the patriarchal throne. Then, in front of the imperial table and in the presence of Photius, divine things were mocked in the most shameful imitation by those contemptible and despicable men. Yet Photius was so far from rebuking them, exposing them, and putting a stop to this most outrageous practice that the lawless man rather confirmed the lawless deed. He prayed that that God-hated "Theophilos", also called Gryllos, whom the utterly uneducated ruler named his own patriarch, might be skilled at mocking in priestly vestments and sacred words, at letting off the loudest noises in the manner of mules, and at having all drink from him, this alone being fit for him to proclaim over them, and at partaking of meats with mustard and vinegar. And with his omophorion the unholy one unholily sealed the unholy hierarchy upon the unholy man, the fool with fools raising his voice in laughter,

mocking the celebrated Ignatius as not accommodating to the times and, as he himself supposed, as being readily blown about by every wind. He even set up a contest with the wretched emperor Michael over which of them could drink more, and beat him by ten cups: when Michael had had his fill at fifty, this Photius drank off sixty and boasted that he was not drunk. 20. Once, when Michael's mother was living in the palace and Gryllos was with him carrying on their lawless doings, Michael pretended that Gryllos was the blessed Ignatius and summoned her to be blessed by him. As she came out with reverence and modesty, she threw herself on the ground, asking for a prayer, for he had so far escaped notice by hiding his beard. Suddenly he leapt up, let off a noise, and added indecent words, among them: "What we have, fires [?], we give to you," and he filled the whole place with stench. She, foretelling the future, [said that he would] go out of the way of God's providence and hand [?]. 21. While Theodora still held the empire, Bogoris, the ruler of Bulgaria, heard that a woman was ruling the empire of the Romans. He sent word to her that he was breaking the treaties and marching against the Romans. She sent back her reply: "You will find me too marching against you, and I hope to master you. And if not, I shall still prevail over you, for the victory will be plainly mine: it will be a woman, not a man, whom you have defeated." For this reason he stayed quiet and renewed the treaties of friendship. 22. She then made inquiry about the monk Theodore Koupharas, who had been taken captive long before. Bogoris took the occasion to ask in turn about his own sister, who had been taken captive and was being kept at the emperor's court. She had learned letters, the Christian way of life, and reverence and praise toward God, and after obtaining her return to her brother she did not cease extolling the faith and urging him to change over to the true faith, though he, held fast by unbelief, refused for a time to look to the truth. But when famine was ravaging his land, he was compelled to cross the borders of the Romans. [23.] In his [?] year the emperor Michael promoted Antigonos, the son of Bardas, to domestic of the Schools. His other son, to whom he gave a wife [?] and who was reviled, he promoted to sole strategos of the West. When he died shortly afterwards, on the Wednesday of Easter Week, Michael promoted his [uncle] Bardas to Caesar. 24. In this year Amer advanced as far as Sinope, plundered all the Roman territory, and returned unharmed. [Note: 'τῆς βασιλείας' P.]

25. In the fourth year of his reign Michael marched out together with the Caesar, by land and by sea, against Gódoris [Boris], ruler of the Bulgarians. When the Bulgarians learned of this, wasting away from famine at the same time, they bowed down as if at the echo of thunder. Before any contest or battle they gave up hope of victory and asked to become Christians and to submit to the emperor of the Romans. The emperor brought them into the City, baptized them all, and gave their ruler the name Michael. When he returned to his own country, he had the Judgment and Retribution painted in his house by a painter called Methodius. For this reason he faced [?] a revolt from his whole nation. With a few men he defeated them, carrying the figure of the divine cross on his breast, and made them all Christians openly. He also wrote to the emperor about land, because his people were cramped in their own territory, while promising to be of one mind with him in the faith for ever and to keep their love unbroken for all ages. The emperor heard this gladly and gave him the land, which was deserted at that time, from Sidera, which was then the boundary between the Romans and them, as far as Debeltos [?], which they call Zagora. 26. In his fifth year, when Amer again marched out against Romania, the generals Petronas and Nasar met him at Lalakaon. Battle was joined and Amer was routed, and the generals brought his head, and the heads of many others, into the City. After this there was a great calm in the East. Yet while the toils and brave deeds of war belonged to others, the emperor's love was poured out on Basil, and he thought that Basil alone was the one who truly served him. 27. In his sixth year he built a stable for his horses, adorning it with marbles and with streams of water of every kind. When it was finished, wishing to be praised, he showed the senseless building to a certain Peter, a learned and mocking man whom they also called Ptochomaches, and said: "I am bound to be remembered for ever for the construction of this work." And Peter said to the emperor: "Justinian built the Great Church and adorned it with gold and silver and precious pearls, and now there is no memory of him. And you, emperor, who have made a dung-heap and a resting place for donkeys, say that you will be remembered for this?" The emperor was enraged at failing to win praise and had him beaten and dragged out. 28. In his seventh year a rumour spread that Bardas the Caesar was having a corrupt affair with his daughter-in-law Eudokia. The patriarch Ignatius often urged him to abstain from this evil. But he did not listen, and instead

was angry [?] with the patriarch, who kept pressing him to live chastely. Once, when Bardas was about to receive communion, the patriarch turned him away as unworthy. Struck in his soul with rage, Bardas drove out the man who had admonished him as a lawless man and a corrupter of the Church, and he subjected him to endless tortures to force him to resign. [For he handed him over to Theodosius, called Moros, to John Gorgonites, and to Nicholas Skoutelops, who shut him naked in the sarcophagus of Copronymus in the winter season. There, under the stress of the cold, he discharged putrid matter and blood from his hidden parts. Enduring these terrible things in this way, that most steadfast man uttered nothing wicked against the Lord. Therefore the Lord raised up Constantine the Armenian to comfort him. Escaping the notice of the evildoers on the spot, he brought the holy man a small jar of wine, bread and apples, and he took him down from the sarcophagus and relieved much of his misery until those men came back. After subjecting the holy man to these things, Bardas the Caesar, since he could not obtain his resignation, ordained Photius the protoasekretis patriarch in his place. He exiled Ignatius to the island of Terebinthos, where he suffered greatly, enduring countless torments every day to make him resign. Then they brought him in chains to Hieria and shut him up in a goat pen. Then they took him to the palace of Promotos [?], and Leo Lalakon crushed his jaws with blows, so that two of his molars fell out. Then they fastened his feet to a murderous iron bar and shut him in a small, narrow cell, and after a few days they confined him in irons at the Noumera. From there they exiled him to the island of Mitylene, and they scattered the metropolitans in prisons, one here, one there. 29. It is also worth saying a little about Photius. This Photius was the son of Sergius the spatharios, whose father was named Zacharias, who in turn had a son Leo, basi[?] . . . For Sergius, who was of [?] blood, burst into a convent of women, carried off a nun from there, stripped her of the habit and took her as his wife. Some time later it happened that Saint Michael of Synada, who was a friend of Sergius, came into his house. Seeing that his wife was pregnant, he thrust out his staff, wishing to strike her, and said: "Would that there were someone able to kill her and the child within her! For I see another Eve led by a serpent, and the child is male. And I see that by God's permission he will become patriarch, to the rejection of the all-venerable and precious cross. He will turn aside to impiety, will bring many to trample on the cross, and will deprive many of the kingdom of heaven by his manifold schemes." Sergius said to him: "If he is going to be such a man, I will kill him together with his mother." The saint answered: "You will not be able to hinder God's permission. Take heed, therefore

30. Then, when he was born, his mother sent for James, abbot of Maximina, and weeping threw the child at his feet, begging that he be baptized by him. For she said: "While I was pregnant I saw in a dream that my belly was split open and a dragon came out. Moreover the holy confessor Hilarion of Dalmatos told me, 'You are carrying Satan incarnate.'" So he took the child and baptized him, naming him Photius and saying, "Perhaps the wrath of God will pass him by." Sergius his father, seeing some [?] in him, said: "Can it be that my wife is the nun the Hebrews expect, who is to give birth to the Antichrist?" Since they were lovers of monks, she would receive monks and ask them to pray for them and for Photius. Once, when this Photius was still [?] a youth, Sergius took him up to Ioannikios, now among the saints, on Olympus, and begged him to pray for him. The old man answered at once: "Photius does not wish in his heart to know your ways, O Lord." Sergius groaned and said: "Why did you say this, father?" The elder said again: "I am showing you what is going to be done by him." Then Sergius covered himself with dust and came down from the mountain. 31. He put him to his studies, and there Photius was more eagerly devoted to Hellenic learning than to the Church's. So he fell in with a certain Hebrew magician, who said: "What will you give me, young man, if I make you have all Greek literature at the tip of your tongue and surpass everyone renowned for wisdom?" He said: "My father will gladly give you half his property." The other replied: "I need no money, and your father must not even know of the matter. But come with me to such-and-such a place and deny the figure on which we nailed Jesus, and I will give you a wonderful amulet, and your whole life will be spent in prosperity and wealth, in great wisdom and joy." He listened eagerly and did everything to please the sorcerer, and from then on he did not keep his mind away from their forbidden books of divination and astrological imposture. He had heard from his father, who had heard it from men of foresight, that by manifold means he would ascend the patriarchal throne. Turning this over in his mind, he made friends with a certain Gregory, who had been bishop of the Church of Syracuse and was also called Asbestas. Gregory had been deposed by the great Methodius for many other reasons, and also for ordaining, outside his own diocese, Zacharias, the presbyter whom the patriarch Methodius had sent to Rome. Photius made friends with him and with certain others deposed on charges, among whom were Eulampius of Apamea, Peter of Sylaion and very many others with them. They gathered in Photius's house and associated with Gregory, plotting against the great Ignatius. A synod of metropolitans and bishops assembled in the patriarchal palace

deposed and anathematized them all. This Photius was ordained patriarch by Bardas the Caesar, the uncle of the emperor Michael. A few days later he asked for the document in his own hand that he had given to the metropolitans when they brought him to ordination, as if he wished to look at something in it. [?] the paper, and a guarantee was sought that it would not be torn up [?]. But Photius's men broke the thumb of the man holding it and snatched the paper away, and Photius got hold of it and tore it into shreds, saying: "I have neither you nor Ignatius as bishop." 32–33. In the second year, as Photius was raising the precious cross at the feast, a clairvoyant monk standing near the altar saw a strange sight: a huge serpent holding Photius's hands, and the precious cross being lifted up upon it. Seized with trembling, he cried out loudly and briefly, "Lord, have mercy!" Some devout men standing with him asked the reason, and he told them the vision. They were among the presbyters of the church, and they said to this devout and clairvoyant monk: "We too, when we celebrate the liturgy with him, have never heard him say a prayer, only whisper the words of the pagan poets. And what is worse, he vomits the foulest vomit underneath the divine and holy table." 34. And John the Hesychast, a God-bearing man truly gifted with foresight, told us: "Once, while I was sitting in deep retreat in the cave, two abbots, Euthymius and Joseph, who were being fiercely persecuted by Photius, came to me. As God gave me, I strengthened them, and finally I said, 'He who endures to the end will be saved,' and sent them away. The following night, before I fell asleep, a great Ethiopian stood beside me, loathsome and terrible to look at, and stretched out his hand to grip my throat and strangle me. At once I made the sign of the cross, took courage, seized him by the hand and said, 'Who are you? What is your name? Who sent you here, and for what reason?' He answered: 'I am the mighty one of Beliar and the servant of Photius. My name is Leoufas [?], fellow-worker of sorcerers and poisoners, guide of adulterers and robbers, friend of the pagans and of my secret servant Photius. The one who has authority over me sent me to avenge him for the insults you heaped on him yesterday, and to work on you so that you would change your mind, accept him, and be estranged from God, as he has done to many others.

But you have made me powerless with the weapon of the cross.' Then I rendered him powerless with the precious cross, and he vanished." 35. One night there happened to be great earthquakes, and Photius himself went up into the ambo to address the people. He said that earthquakes come not from the multitude of sins but from an excess of water, and that every man has two souls, one which sins and the other which does not sin. Hearing this, the protoasekretis went and told the emperor: "Our servants are pressing us, saying: 'We supposed we had one soul, and each month we received two modii apiece. But now, as the patriarch openly teaches, each man has two souls, so add another two modii for us.'" The emperor laughed and said: "Is that how the Khazar-face lays down doctrine?" So he immediately summoned the patriarch and asked him, as if angry: "Is that what you teach, Marzoukas, that a man has two souls?" But Photius craftily won him over with plausible arguments and persuaded him that he had said it about other matters, not in that sense. Gregory of Syracuse asked him: "What does 'Marzoukas' mean?" He said: "Mar is dog; zou is dragging [?]; kas is kassyma, leather. That is, a dog dragging a hide." 36. A certain artisan who lived at the Sophiai, as those who saw and heard it have confirmed, lay at the point of death for many days, eating away his tongue, lips and hands, and he could not die. Recovering a little, he said: "Know, brothers, that the patriarch Photius taught me not to receive communion fasting. That is why I suffer what you see, and cannot die." And having said this, he breathed his last. So much for Photius. 37. In his ninth year the emperor Michael marched out against the Hagarenes, leaving Ooryphas behind as eparch in the City. When the emperor had already reached Mauropotamos, Ooryphas informed him of the arrival of the Rus, who had two hundred ships. The emperor at once turned back, having accomplished nothing at all. 38. In his tenth year the Rus came within the Hieron and wrought great slaughter. Then they surrounded the City. The emperor barely managed to cross over, and he and the patriarch Photius at once went to the church of the Theotokos at Blachernae. With hymns they brought out the holy maphorion of the Theotokos and dipped its hem into the sea. Though there was a dead calm, at once gusts of wind arose, and though the sea had been still, wave upon wave rose up, and the ships of the godless Rus were wrecked. Few escaped the danger [?].

[?] . . . as he was coming in. The patrikios Damianos, who was also parakoimomenos, was sitting in the Horologion and did not rise to honour him. Angered, he went weeping to the emperor and reported this, saying: "To the disgrace of your majesty he did not rise for me." That very hour the emperor exiled the parakoimomenos Damianos to St Mamas and promoted Basil, his protostrator, to parakoimomenos. When the Caesar saw this he was deeply grieved, and he sought to kill

40. In his eleventh year the emperor Michael separated Basil from his wife Maria and gave him Eudokia Ingerina as his wife, laying down that he should have her as his lawful wife. For she was the emperor's concubine, and he loved her greatly for her beauty. To Basil's former wife Maria he gave gold and great wealth and sent her back to her own people. And he joined his own sister Thekla to Basil, for Basil to have privately. Now the Caesar and Basil eyed each other with suspicion, each looking for a way to destroy the other. So Basil slandered the Caesar to the emperor as plotting against him, but the emperor heard this as nonsense. So, eager to convince the emperor, Basil made friends with Symbatios, patrikios and logothete of the drome, the Caesar's son-in-law, and they confirmed their agreement with each other by oaths. Basil assured Symbatios with dreadful oaths: "The emperor loves you very much and wishes to make you Caesar, but because of your father-in-law he cannot bring it about." Deceived by this, Symbatios turned against the Caesar Bardas, his own father-in-law. He went in to the emperor and swore, assuring him: "The Caesar wants to kill you," and he revealed the details of the plot as well. The emperor, persuaded by Symbatios's oaths and confirmed by Basil's words, harboured a grudge against the Caesar. Basil had prepared everything against the Caesar, but since he could do nothing in the City, he persuaded the emperor to launch a fleet against Crete. While this was under way, Leo the Philosopher urged the Caesar to hold back and guard himself against Basil. The Caesar in turn called on the emperor to keep clear of Basil. Since the procession for the Annunciation was being held at the Chalkoprateia, when the Gospel had been read, the patriarch Photius and the emperor, with the Caesar and Basil the parakoimomenos, went up to the Catechumena. While the patriarch held in his hands the precious body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, the emperor and Basil dipped their pens and signed the precious crosses, confirming by oath that the Caesar could go with them on the expedition without fear. But Leo the Philosopher openly warned Bardas not to set out with them, and as he was setting out told him he would not come back.

41. Signs had also attended his death. For when an earthquake took place, the statue that stood second on a column near St Anne's fell. When this was reported by the Caesar to Leo the Philosopher, he interpreted it to mean that the second after the first ruler would fall through death. Then there was a garment sent to him by his sister Theodora, which fell short of the proper length and had a partridge embroidered on it in gold. When he received it he asked her why it had been cut short. In my opinion, says the writer, she foreshadowed the outcome in both respects: by the partridge she hinted at the treachery against him, and by the shortness at the shortness of his days. He also saw a dream like this. It seemed that on a feast day the Caesar went with the emperor to God's Holy Sophia in the customary splendour. When they were at the holy altar, angels in shining robes appeared to them, and toward the inner sanctuary someone was seen above, an old man enthroned, and this was Peter the apostle. Ignatius was kneeling before him in tears, reminding him of what he had endured under abuse. Peter, moved with him by his suffering, said that he would obtain vengeance from the hand of the Lord. At once he handed a sword to one of the two gold-clad men standing beside him like praepositi, and said [?]. Quickly nodding, he set the emperor apart on the right, and the God-hated Caesar, so he said, on the left, to be punished limb by limb with the sword. As this was being carried out [?], he declared that Michael too should await the cutting, calling him a child of impiety [?]. 42. After Easter the emperor set out with a large army and came to the theme of the Thrakesians, and Basil was plotting against the Caesar. In the plot were his brother Marianos, Symbatios the Caesar's son-in-law, Bareis the brother of Symbatios, Peter the Bulgarian, his cousin Leo the Assyrian, John Chaldos and Constantine Toxaras. John Neatokomites found out about this and informed the Caesar through Prokopios. But the Caesar said to him: "You are young, and you talk nonsense, stirring up [?]." Yet the Caesar spent the night sleepless, and at early dawn he summoned all his men, explained what he had been told, and asked for advice. Philotheos, protospatharios and genikos, who was dear to him, said to the Caesar: "Tomorrow, master, put on your gold-embroidered tunic and show yourself to your enemies, and they will flee from before your face." When the sun rose he mounted his horse and came to the emperor's tent in splendid dress, with many people around him. Basil came, took him by the hand and led him in to the emperor. He said to the emperor: "Now that the whole army has been gathered, master, give the order to cross over to Crete." And at once Basil, standing behind him, gave him with

…sword. The rest hacked him limb from limb while the emperor looked on in silence. It was about the third hour. At once they went back to the City. When they reached the market of Akritas, a monk standing on a high rock shouted loudly at the emperor: “A fine campaign you have made, O emperor, killing your own kinsman! Woe to you for doing these things!” The emperor and Basil were enraged and sent men to kill the monk. But the bystanders persuaded the man who had been sent that the monk was a fool and possessed by a demon, and so the monk only barely escaped punishment.

43. On holy Pentecost, in Hagia Sophia, Emperor Michael and Patriarch Photius crowned Basil the parakoimomenos emperor. Michael had a tomos read out by Castor the asekretis, which ran as follows: “Bardas the Caesar plotted to kill me, and for this reason he drew me out of the City. Had it not been revealed to me by Symbatius and Basil, I would not be among the living. He has therefore died through his own sin. Basil the parakoimomenos is faithful, he guards my reign, he has freed me from my enemy, and he has great love for me. It is my wish that he be the guardian and steward of my reign, and that he be acclaimed by all as emperor.” And all acclaimed: “Many years to Michael and Basil!” Castor the asekretis, who had read the tomos, went off to Nicomedia, came to a monastery of men and stayed in the middle of a meadow. There was a well there, and he fell into it and drowned.

44. Symbatius, the son-in-law of the Caesar, saw that Basil had made a fool of him and was moved to hatred against him. He took counsel with George Peganes and asked to be appointed strategos, and so it was done. In his place Goumer was promoted logothete of the drome. Symbatius and Peganes went out together and ravaged the people and set the countryside on fire (for it was summer), acclaiming Michael alone and denouncing Basil. When the emperors learned of this, they wrote to the other strategoi to make war on them. Nikephoros Maleinos spread written messages among the whole army, so that they could seize the two by guile and not fall into civil war. So Peganes was seized, brought into the City and blinded, and they set him in the Milion to beg. Symbatius too was seized by Maleinos at Keltzene. When he was brought to St Mamas, they brought out Peganes with an earthenware censer smoking with brimstone, and he went to meet Symbatius and censed him. Symbatius too was blinded, in one eye, and they cut off his right hand and set him as well to beg, at the place of Tzausios. After three days they brought the two of them into the City to their own houses.

45. Then Emperor Michael, through the engineer called Damaris, threw Constantine the

Kaballinos out of his tomb, and John the impious patriarch too out of his tomb, together with his omophorion. Through the eparch he had them shut up in the praetorium, and on a day of horse-races he brought them out, stripped them and had them flogged with whips, and he burned their bones in the Mauriana. The sarcophagus of Copronymus, which was green and marvellous, he had sawn up and made into balustrades in the church he had built in the palace of the Pharos.

46. In the month of September of the fifteenth indiction Emperor Constantine was born to Michael and Eudokia Ingerina, while Michael was still alive. When there was a race at St Mamas, the emperor drove for the Blues; Constantine the Armenian, father of the patrician Thomas and of Genesios the drungarios of the Watch, for the Whites; Agallianos for the Greens; and Krasos for the Reds. The emperor won. And what came of this? This too belongs to the wickedness of Emperor Michael, showing how far he diminished the strength of the Romans. Leo the philosopher, who became archbishop of Thessalonica, had advised Emperor Theophilus and made two clocks that kept exactly the same time. One he placed at the fortress in Cilicia near Tarsus, and the other was kept in the palace. On them was written, for each hour, what might happen in Syria: at the first hour, for instance, whether there had been a Saracen raid; at the second, whether there was war; at the third, whether there was a fire; at the fourth, whether something else had happened; and likewise for the rest. So if any of the twelve written cases occurred in Syria, a beacon was lit there at the hour that matched the case, since the men on watch kept their eyes closely and precisely on the marks engraved on the clocks. The beacon at once passed the signal from the fortress called Loulon to those on Mount Argaios, then to those at Samos and those at Aigilon, then to those on Mount Mamas, from there to Kyrizos, then to Mokilos, and from there the mount of St Auxentios quickly made it plain to the attendants assigned to the duty in the palace, at the terrace of the Pharos. Now while Emperor Michael was racing, as has been said, the beacon signalled a Saracen raid. But so that the spectators of the hippodrome should not lose interest the next day, he ordered that such beacons no longer be used.

47. So, as has been said, when the emperor had won and sat down to dinner with Basil and Eudokia, the patrician Basiliskianos praised him for driving the chariot so skilfully. At once the emperor ordered him to stand up, pull off the emperor's boots and put them on himself. Basiliskianos refused and looked at Basil, but since the emperor gave the order angrily and Basil nodded, he put them on. Then the emperor said to Basil, with an oath: “They suit him better. For

do I not have the power to make another man emperor, just as I made you emperor?” And he grew angry and raged against Basil. Eudokia said to the emperor in tears: “The dignity of your majesty, my lord, is a great thing, and we too have been honoured with it though unworthy. It is not right that it be treated with contempt.” But he said to Basil: “Do not be upset at this. I want to make Basiliskianos emperor too.” And to those present he said: “Is it not fitting for him to be emperor?

First, a form worthy of sovereign rule;
Second, a crown [?] that sits naturally on him for the city.
All things fit him for the dignity.

How much better, then, that I should make him emperor!” Basil, in anger and great grief…

48. When the emperor went out hunting, a monk gave Basil a paper revealing the plot that the emperor was hatching against him: the emperor had ordered one of his shield-bearers to hurl his lance at Basil. At dinnertime, not only on this occasion but on others too, once Michael was drunk on wine he would give orders of unspeakable cruelty, having ears, noses and heads cut off. Had not some, moved by pity, neglected these orders and put them off until the next day, expecting him to call them back and repent, as indeed happened, everyone who stayed with Michael would have perished. Basil too had often been the plaything of his drunken insolence, but he endured it and waited for the man to have some change of heart. At last, growing suspicious of how things stood, he hastened to strike first rather than be killed by him. When Michael's mother Theodora invited the emperor to the Anthemiou palace, Basil laid his plans against Michael. Then, when the emperor sat down to dinner, he invited Eudokia and Basil to dine with him. When the emperor had drunk a great deal of wine, Basil got up as if to relieve himself, went into the emperor's bedchamber and, being strong, bent the bolts of the doors so that the doors could not be locked. Then he went back and dined with the emperor again. Afterwards Emperor Michael got up, but he was so drunk that he could not walk, and Basil led him by the hand to his bedchamber, kissed his hand and went out. Inside the bedchamber was Basiliskianos, sleeping by the emperor's order in the bed of Rentakios the parakoimomenos, to guard him. The koitonites Ignatius went to lock the door of the bedchamber, found it bent, and in despair sat down on the bed tearing out his hair. While the emperor lay in a wine-sodden sleep like death, Basil suddenly arrived with his companions and opened the doors. Ignatius came out in fear and tried to stop Basil from going in. At that moment the emperor woke up, and at once John Chaldos cut off his hands. The apelates Iakobitzes wounded Basiliskianos with his sword and threw him

down. The others stood outside on guard. When both had been dealt with [?], Asylaion said to Basil: “Even if we have cut off his hands, we have still left him alive. And if he lives, what defence shall we make?” He turned back, plunged his sword into the emperor's heart and spilled out his entrails. There was a storm at sea, but they gathered together and came as far as the crossing, climbed up by the wall and came to the palace. A slab was blocking the wall; Basil, holding on to two of his men, kicked the slab and broke it, and went in as far as the gate of the palace. Eulogios the Persian, who was with Basil, said in his own language to Artabasdos the hetaireiarch: “Michael has died by the sword; open to Basil.” Artabasdos ran to the papias, took the keys from him by force and opened up. Once inside, Basil took the keys of the palace into his own hands. These things happened on the third day, in the year 6366, at the third hour of the night, in the first indiction, on the night before the feast of Thecla the protomartyr. At dawn he made Gregory, son of Philemon, papias, and immediately sent to St Mamas and brought Eudokia, daughter of Inger, into the palace with great pomp. He also sent John the praipositos to take the Dekapolitissa back to her parents, and Paul, the official in charge of the bedchamber, to bury Michael. Paul went and found him wrapped in the saddle-cloth of the right-hand horse of the team he used to drive, with his mother and sister mourning and lamenting over him. He put him in a small boat, took him across to the monastery of Chrysopolis and buried him.

Basil, Orthodox Emperor of the Romans, 19 years.

In the year of the world 6370 [?], and of the divine incarnation 862, Basil became Orthodox emperor of the Romans for 19 years. In bodily appearance he was in the very bloom of health, robust, with eyebrows that met, fine eyes and a sullen look, dark-complexioned, of middling height verging on tall, broad-chested, with downcast eyes, and, as one might guess, always brooding over his own affairs. He came from Adrianople in Macedonia, which was formerly called Orestias after Orestes son of Agamemnon. Orestes, moved by just zeal over Clytemnestra's treacherous murder of his father, killed her together with Aegisthus and went quite mad; but he bathed at the confluence of the three rivers, the Hebrus, the Arzos and the Artakos, and was freed from his sickness. There he built this city and called it by his own name. Hadrian Caesar enlarged it with well-built fortifications and renamed it the city of Hadrian. It lies three days' journey for a nimble traveller on the road from Constantinople [?], embraced by Mount Haemus, beside which the three rivers, as in the Homeric line, “into a meeting of ravines pour together their mighty water.”

2. This emperor gave orders to Marianos the eparch, the son of Petronas, and had himself proclaimed sole emperor. Oryphas, who held the rank of strategos and commander of the fleet, understood what Basil had done and, being loyal to his master, was moved to avenge Emperor Michael. The autocrator summoned him and at first threatened him with insulting words, but then judged him worthy of approval, since he had chosen to dare such things on behalf of his master. And indeed, as time went on, Basil came to trust him so fully that he left the City in his charge when he went out against the enemy.

3. It is also necessary to record the vengeance that came from God upon those who had done away with Michael. Iakobitzes was hunting with the emperor when his sword fell. As he was about to dismount to pick it up, his foot caught in the stirrup, and his horse, taking fright, dragged him over ravines and cliffs and tore him limb from limb. John Chaldos became strategos of Chaldia; when he was caught plotting against the emperor, he was impaled by Andrew the stratelates. The emperor's brother Asylaion was banished by the emperor to his suburban estate; being harsh and cruel to his slaves, he was killed by them with knives. The emperor seized them, hacked them limb from limb and burned them in the Amastrianon. The apelates, the son of the Persian, was eaten by worms and gave up his soul. Constantine Toxaras was cut down with swords among the Kibyrrhaiots and died; and Marianos, the emperor's brother, broke his foot and, eaten by worms, died.

4. On the feast of Christ's Nativity, when the procession took place, the emperor had Photius baptize his son Stephen in the Great Church.

5. In his third year, on the feast of St Polyeuktos, there was an earthquake lasting forty days and forty nights, and many churches collapsed, among them the church of the all-holy Theotokos called the Sigma, so that everyone singing there was killed. Leo the philosopher happened to be there and urged them all to leave, but those who were not persuaded all perished. The philosopher himself was saved, together with two others, by standing against a column under a cross-beam [?], and only nine others survived, under the ambo.

6. When the emperor came to the church and was about to receive communion, Patriarch Photius called him a robber and a murderer, unworthy of the divine communion. The emperor was enraged and sent to Rome, brought back a tomos with Roman bishops, and drove Photius from the throne; and he raised Ignatius, now among the saints, to the patriarchate a second time.

7. After Photius had been expelled from the church and exiled to the monastery of Skepe, he devised a fabrication of the following kind. He cast the horoscope of Emperor

Basil, making out that he traced his descent from Tiridates, ruler of Great Armenia, and arranged for the book to be placed in the imperial library through Theophanes called Sphenodaimon, who was then an imperial cleric and attached to Basil on account of his wisdom and learning. He took the first letters of the names Basil, Eudokia, Constantine, Leo, Alexander and Stephen, and read together they spelled the name Beklas. He worked out this man's genealogy from the beginning, both by place and by deeds, wrote it up in the book, and by various artifices made the book look very old; then, as has been said, he deposited it in the imperial library through Theophanes Sphenodaimon. One day Sphenodaimon was searching for some book by imperial order; when he came upon this one and, after examining it closely, was at a loss, he showed it to the emperor and said: “No one but Photius can understand what is written in this.” At once Photius was sent for, and his excuse was ready to hand: “Unless I see the emperor, I will not say what the book is or what its title means.” He came in and read it, and claimed he had learned it as if from an angel. This in turn brought about Photius's return to intimacy with the emperor.

8. In his fifth year, on 23 November, Emperor Alexander was born of Eudokia, daughter of Inger, a legitimate son of Basil. The emperor campaigned against the Hagarenes in Africa, fought many battles, was defeated in all of them and lost many of the Romans. When the emperor himself was about to be captured, Theophylaktos Abastaktos, the father of Romanos who later became emperor, saved him. When the emperor returned to the City, he sent his son-in-law Christopher to Africa, who won a victory, sacked it and razed it to the ground.

9. In his sixth year the patriarch Ignatius made the church of Satyros into a church dedicated to the Archistrategos Anatellon; later he also turned it into a monastery of men, where he was buried. It is called Satyros because, a short distance from this monastery, there is an old place called Satyros, where there was a temple built by the Greeks to that same Satyr; because the monastery is near it, it is called by the same name. From that temple Emperor Theophilus took the materials when he built the palace of Bryas. It is called Anatellon for the following reason. Once, when Emperor Nikephoros was hunting in the area where the monastery now stands, a deer was caught at the very spot where the altar of the monastery is now set up, and there was found an old table supported on a column, bearing this inscription: “This is the holy altar of the Archistrategos Michael Anatellon, which the holy apostle Andrew set up.”

10. In his seventh and eighth years Basil baptized all the Hebrews under his rule, giving them

ranks and many gifts. At that time he also made the Nicholas mentioned earlier, the prosmonarios of St Diomedes, oikonomos and synkellos; his brother John drungarios of the Watch; another brother, Paul, head of the imperial sakelle; and another brother, Constantine, genikos logothete.

11. In his ninth year the emperor began to build the New Church, and Syracuse was surrendered to the Saracens.

12. In his tenth year Niketas Xylenites, the epi tes trapezes, was accused of being the Augusta's lover; he was tonsured and became a monk. The emperor broke up many bronze works for the sake of the New Church, and he also took marble, mosaic tesserae and columns from many churches and houses for it. Among these was a bronze statue standing in the Senate in the form of a bishop, which held in its hand a staff with a serpent coiled around it. They brought it to the vestiarion. The emperor came and put his finger into the serpent's mouth, and inside was another serpent, a living one, which bit the emperor's finger, and he was cured only with difficulty by antidotes. He also had the statue of Solomon that stood in the Basilica recast in his own likeness, and offered himself as a sacrifice to God in the foundations of the New Church.

13. In his eleventh year he again campaigned against the Melitenians, won many battles, took many captives and returned.

14. In his twelfth year the patriarch Ignatius died, and Photius was raised to the throne again.

15. In his thirteenth year the emperor campaigned against Germanikeia, took its people captive and returned. Constantine died, the son of Michael by Eudokia, though, as the story goes, he was Basil's son. Basil mourned him deeply and laid him in the tombs of the emperors.

16. In his fourteenth year, on 1 May, the New Church was consecrated and its altar installed by the patriarch Photius.

17. In his fifteenth year Leo Salibaras introduced to Patriarch Photius the monk Theodore Santabarenos, who later became archbishop of Euchaita through him, presenting him as pious, a worker of wonders and gifted with foresight. Photius in turn commended him to Basil. The emperor was pleased with him (for Theodore went along with his desires) and held him in great honour. The emperor was despondent over the death of his son Constantine, out of the affection he had for him, and Theodore deceived him and promised to show him the boy alive. And so he did: as the emperor was passing through a thicket, an apparition was contrived [on horseback?], clothed in gold-woven garments and in the form of Constantine. The emperor saw it with his own eyes, embraced it and kissed it. And when it had vanished, him…

…he supposed he had to…, and that he had not been deceived. For this reason he also built a monastery there and named it after Saint Constantine. 18. With these and a great many other tricks, being thoroughly initiated in the arts of Apollonius, Santabarenos made the emperor place great trust in him. This notorious Santabarenos was made bishop of Euchaita by Photius himself during Photius's second usurpation. He was the son of a Manichaean and a Manichaean himself. As a young man he escaped capital punishment through the Caesar Bardas and was handed over to the monastery of Stoudios for correction. But though he put on the monastic habit, he did not turn back from his wickedness at all. During Photius's first usurpation he became abbot of that very monastery, and because of him all the pious monks of the monastery fled, refusing to accept communion with Photius. But when Photius was driven from the patriarchate, that man with Satan in his name was also expelled from the monastery. Then he attached himself to Photius and said: "Make use of one of the men of the emperor's bedchamber. Take these waters that I have prepared and [?sprinkle them] in the bedchamber, and you will at once see the emperor enslaved to love for you. After this, work to bring it about that I [?see] him, and I will make you return to your former honour." When this had been done, very early the next morning the emperor sent his sons to Photius for a blessing, and gold as well. He settled him in the Magnaura, conversed with him constantly, and granted him such freedom of speech that all Photius's household were appointed to offices in the palace. From that point Photius introduced the arch-magician Santabarenos to the emperor [P. 458] as holy, pious and gifted with the keenest second sight, and won him the emperor's favour. 19. In his sixteenth year the emperor took a wife for the emperor Leo, Theophano the daughter of Martinakios. He had them crowned and held the wedding in the Magnaura. 20. In his seventeenth year the fleets of the Saracens attacked Italy, Sicily and the other lands, and something like the following came of it. [?] The leader of the Hagarenes seized Bari, a great city of the Ragusans [?], settled in it, and ravaged many other cities and territories. So the emperor wrote to the king of Francia to support the fleet he had sent against the Hagarenes. War was waged, and the fortress and the territory were taken, and so were Saldanos himself and the people under him. The king [?] took this man away to Capua, [?] and living with the king he enjoyed freedom of speech and shared his table [?]. But being cunning, he tried to secure his own safety by slandering others. He said in secret to the rulers of Capua and Benevento: "I want to tell you a secret plan of the king's, but I fear the danger of being exposed."

When they swore to keep what was said to themselves, he said: "The king is shortly going to send all of you in iron chains to his own land of Francia." They did not believe him and asked for clearer proof. So Saldanos went back to the king and told him: "Your hold on these fortresses is not secure as long as their rulers live here. If you want to rule the land firmly, send them in chains to Francia." The king was persuaded and ordered chains to be forged at once, as though for some urgent need. When Saldanos saw this, he said to the rulers: "Do you still not believe me?" Seeing that the barbarian was telling the truth, the rulers looked for a way to defend themselves against the king. When he went out hunting, they shut the gates against him, and he went back to his own land in grief. Saldanos then demanded his reward for the information, and the reward was permission to go back to his own homeland. Having recovered his own realm, and not giving up his wickedness, he marched against Capua and Benevento. They sent envoys to the king, but were sent away with insults. So they sent to the emperor. He quickly sent the envoy back, announcing that they should expect help from him shortly. The bearer of the message fell into the hands of the enemy. Saldanos said to him: "If you do what I want, you will be spared and receive many gifts." When he agreed, Saldanos said: "I want you to stand outside the fortress and tell those inside: 'I have carried out my mission, but do not expect help from the emperor, for he did not listen to your plea.'" The man came near the wall with Saldanos's attendants, asked for the leading men of the city to come, and said: "Although my death is plain before me and slaughter is at hand, I will still not hide the truth. Only I ask and implore you to repay the favour to my children and my wife. For, my lords, though I am now held in the hands of the enemy, I carried out my mission and brought your embassy to the emperor of the Romans, and you may expect help from him shortly. So stand firm and nobly and do not lose heart, for one is coming who will rescue you, even if he does not rescue me." When Saldanos's men heard this, they were enraged at the trick and at once cut him to pieces with their swords. But Saldanos, fearing the force expected from the emperor, lifted the siege and went back to his own land. 21. In his eighteenth year the emperor Leo was denounced to his own father by Santabarenos, in the following way. Leo was sensible and lived a pious life, and he condemned what Santabarenos was doing, rebuked him and shunned him. Santabarenos could not bear to be hated like this, and he suspected that Leo would denounce him to the emperor. So what did he contrive? He had a large knife made, the kind called a paramerion, and fitted it out

[759] [?] elaborately, and gave it to Leo, saying: "I know that when you hunt, an animal often falls into your hands while you are alone, and because you have no knife to kill it, it gets away. So carry this. Perhaps the emperor your father will praise you for it too." Persuaded by the villain, Leo took the knife. Then the treacherous Santabarenos went off and denounced him to his father: "Your son Leo is carrying a paramerion, and when he goes out [?] with you, he means to kill you." When the emperor heard this, he searched Leo and found it. He shut him up in the Margarites, intending to blind him, and would have done so had Photius the patriarch and many other members of the senate not prevented it. [P. 460] He severely punished all Leo's men, and since nothing in the accusation was found to be true, he exiled them. Leo spent three months out of sight, lamenting and weeping and pleading with the emperor in many letters. When the feast of the holy Elijah came, Leo was reconciled, because the emperor had great faith in that saint, and it happened in this way. In the palace there hung a bird in a woven cage, a mimic able to make many sounds, called a parrot. Whether someone had taught it or it had learned in some other way, it often cried out: "Alas, alas, lord Leo!" Once, when the emperor was holding a banquet and the leading members of the council were dining with him, the bird kept crying out these words. The guests grew gloomy [?], stopped feasting, and sat lost in thought. Noticing them, the emperor asked the reason. Filled with tears, they said: "What sort of food shall we be seen to eat, when we, who are thought to be rational and devoted to our master, are reproached like this by the voice of a creature without reason? It calls for its own master, while we in our luxury have forgotten our master who has done no wrong. If he is proven guilty and to have raised his hand against his father's head, let us all kill him with our own hands, and let us never have our fill of his blood. But how long will the slanderous tongue prevail against him?" Softened by these words, the emperor told them to sit down for the time being and promised to look into the matter. Not long afterwards, coming back to his natural feelings, he brought Leo out of custody and into his presence, changed his mourning clothes, ordered the excess of the hair that had grown during his grief to be cut off, and restored him to his former rank and honour as emperor. When the procession of the holy Elijah took place, the people saw him and cried out: "Glory to you, O God!" And the emperor said: "Glorify God for my son. You are going to suffer many afflictions from him and pass through painful days." 22. In his nineteenth year a revolt was plotted by [Note 75: for "how long", read "but if not, how long" [?]. Note 76: the common text reads "painful".]

John Kourkouas, domestic of the Hikanatoi, after he had received an oracle from the recluse at Blachernae. With him were as many as sixty-six officers, among them Michael the hetaireiarch, Katoudes, Myxiares and Babutzikos. [P. 461] The emperor arrested them all, had them flogged in the Hippodrome and shaved, and had the remaining hair burned. Then he paraded them in disgrace and exiled them. 23. Once, when the emperor had gone out hunting, a huge stag appeared and lifted him from his horse by his belt with its antler. Someone rushed up, cut the belt with his sword and rescued him. After they returned, the emperor had him beheaded, saying: "Do not bare a sword against an emperor." Basil fell ill from the mauling by the stag and died. He told his son and successor Leo, and Stylianos, the guardian of the emperor's sons: "The unholy Photius and his fellow initiate Santabarenos estranged me from God and made me a stranger to true knowledge, and so they have dragged me into the same punishment as theirs." With these words he died, leaving Leo, Stephen and Alexander. Leo, emperor of the Romans, 25 years and 9 months. Year of the world 6388, of the divine Incarnation 888 [?]. Leo, emperor of the Romans, 25 years and 9 months. His brother Stephen was a cleric and served as synkellos to the patriarch Photius, who had brought him up and educated him. After Leo became sole ruler, he sent Andrew the stratelates to Chrysopolis with many candles and with clergy and senators. With great zeal and honour and with hymns, Andrew brought back the remains of the emperor Michael and laid them in a sarcophagus in the church of the Holy Apostles. Leo exposed Photius the patriarch as a plotter against the Church, expelled him, and confined him in the monastery in the Armeniakon theme called Gordon's, where he also died. He had his own brother Stephen the synkellos ordained by Theophanes the protothronos and the other bishops. Stephen lived [as patriarch] 6 years and 5 months, and was buried in the monastery of the Sykai. There was a fire near the Sophiai and the Sidera, and the church of Saint Thomas was burned as well, which Leo himself splendidly restored. [P. 462] He brought Theodore Santabarenos from Euchaita to the city. Andrew the domestic and Stephen the magistros brought charges against him and Photius, claiming that they had slandered the emperor Leo to his father the emperor Basil. The senate condemned them, and they left Photius at Gordon's, but had Santabarenos flogged and exiled to Athens. Then the emperor sent men after him, had him blinded and exiled him to the East. Many years later, being entreated, he brought him back into the city and ordered him to receive provisions from the Nea [?]

…in all the themes. When battle was joined, only Constantine himself barely managed to escape, while the others were slaughtered or captured. There was also an eclipse of the sun, so that it was night for three hours and the stars were visible. There were also violent winds, lightning and thunder, and seven people were burned by them in the Forum. 3. In his third year the fortress of Samos was besieged by the Hagarenes, and its general Paspalas was taken captive. Having become attached to Zoe, the daughter of Zaoutzes, the emperor appointed Zaoutzes basileopator, coining the title himself. Symeon, the ruler of Bulgaria, marched against the Romans. He was attacked and defeated by the Turks, and the emperor bought back all the captives. Then Symeon routed the Turks in turn, recovered his captives by request, and made peace. Shortly afterwards the peace was broken again, and a battle was fought at Bulgarophygon. There was a general rout and everyone perished, including the protovestiarios Theodore. When the patriarch Stephen died, Antony, called [?], was ordained patriarch in his place.

4. In his seventh year the people of Cherson killed their general. The fortress of Koron in Cappadocia was also taken by the Hagarenes. The emperor Leo went out on an excursion to Damianos's estate, accompanied by the regent Zaoutzes and his daughter Zoe, who was with the emperor (for his first wife Theophano was staying at the Holy Soros of Blachernae, devoted to prayer). There Zaoutzes's relatives, the tzantzes and the others, plotted to murder the emperor. [P. 463] Zoe was sleeping with the emperor, and when she sensed the danger she woke him. They crossed at once by boat to Pegai, and early in the morning he quickly entered the palace. 5. In this year the Augusta Theophano died, having reigned for 12 years. Not many days later God revealed her as a worker of miracles, because she had been free of jealousy and resentment and had devoted herself to God ceaselessly in almsgiving and prayer. The emperor Leo crowned his second wife Zoe, the daughter of Zaoutzes, and received the marriage blessing with her from a cleric named Sinoupes. The man who gave the blessing was deposed. She reigned 1 year and 8 months and died. They found a sarcophagus to lay her body in, and inside it letters were carved that read: "Daughter of Babylon, the wretched one." Near [?] he built a church of Saint Zoe and laid her in it. And near the Holy Apostles the emperor Leo bought up houses and built a very beautiful church in the name of his first wife Theophano, and laid her there too.

6. In his ninth year a plot against the emperor Leo was hatched by Zaoutzes's relatives. It was detected, and he arrested and exiled them all, and wiped out Zaoutzes's whole family. 7. In his tenth year the patriarch Antony died, and Nicholas, the emperor's mystikos, was ordained patriarch. At that time Demetrias was also taken by Damianos the Hagarene. The emperor crowned Anna, the daughter of Zoe, Zaoutzes's daughter, because he could not hold the customary banquets while there was no Augusta. 8. In his eleventh year the emperor took a third wife, Eudokia from the Opsikion, and had her crowned and proclaimed. She bore him a son and died, and the child that was born also died. 9. In his thirteenth year the emperor built a church of Saint Lazarus at the place called Topoi, and established a monastery for eunuch monks there. In it he laid the bodies of Saint Lazarus and of Mary Magdalene. At this time Taormina was handed over to the Hagarenes. 10. In the fifteenth year the island of Lemnos was taken by the

[P. 464] 11. In the sixteenth year, during the Pentecost procession, the emperor was entering Saint Mokios, which they say was formerly a temple of Heracles. When he came near the solea, someone came out of the ambo and struck him on the head with a heavy, thick staff. Had the staff not been caught on a chandelier, it would have killed him on the spot. As the blood poured out, there was confusion and the officials fled. And because his brother Alexander had pleaded illness and not come down for the entrance, suspicion arose that he had contrived the attack. The man who struck the emperor was seized. For many days he endured many tortures and punishments, but since he named no one, his hands and feet were cut off and he was burned in the Sphendone of the Hippodrome. From then on that procession was abolished. Some time later Mark, the most learned oikonomos of that church, who had completed Lord Kosmas's four-ode canon for Great Week [?], that is, for Great Saturday, went up to the emperor. While dining with him, he begged him not to abolish the feast. When the emperor refused, Mark said that this had been foretold by David, for he says: "How much evil the enemy has done in your holy place, and those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast." "And you, master, are to hold the empire for ten years from now." And that is what happened, for he died on the very same day of the year on which he was struck.

12. In the seventeenth year the emperor took a fourth wife as well, Zoe, called Karbonopsina. 13. In the eighteenth year the fleet of the Hagarenes came up against the city, together with the Tripolite. The Tripolites got their name because they were gathered from three peoples, settlers from Arados, Tyre and Sidon. In the same way the Aegean Sea took its name from the movement of its waters, which dart like a goat. Likewise Strobelos was named from the lie of the place, and Lampsakos from a shining light. When the Phocaeans were founding the city at night and praying, a light shone on them from heaven, and the base of its foundations was made firm. And Imbros is named after Imbros, son of

…whose father was Staphylus, the beloved son of Dionysus. [P. 465] The Hellespont is named after Helle, the sister of Phrixus, who was cast into the sea there. Kibyrrha is named after Kibyrrhos, the brother [?]. Thasos was formerly called Chryse. Samothrace was a peninsula in Thrace. It used to be called Therioussa because it was full of wild beasts, and it was sacred to the nymphs. Later the current broke through and it became an island. When Samian settlers took possession of it, it was renamed Samothrace. Laodicea was named after the wife of Seleucus son of Antiochus, who founded Laodicea and named it after her. Tenedos is named after Tennes, son of Kyknos son of Poseidon, and after the seat of Athena's temple on it [?]. Mesembria was formerly Menebria [?], from Menas [?] the Thracian who founded it, and from "bria," which among some Thracians means a town. For the sake of a smoother sound it is now called Mesembria. Haemus is named after someone killed there by Heracles, who stained the place with his blood; it is a promontory of Thrace. Medeia is named after Mede, the daughter of Aeetes. Selymbria is named after Selys, king of the Thracians, who founded it. Macedonia was formerly called Emathia, after an ancient ruler. There was also a city by the sea called Emathia, which gave its name to the people. Nicopolis is named after the victory that Augustus Sebastos won over Antony and Cleopatra, by which he brought the realm of the Egyptians under the Romans. The Hieron of the Euxine was set up by the sailors of the Argo as they passed by there. A pharos is a structure on which a beacon is placed, to guide travellers at night safely. The Rhos, who are also called Dromitai, are named after a certain mighty Rhos, after they had escaped the consequences [?] of what was said by those who consulted [?], through some warning or divine inspiration, and who had overpowered them [?]. They got the name Dromitai because they run swiftly. They are of the race of the Franks. The hill called Trikephalos in the Opsikion is so named because its shape has three heads, just as Rhadenos is named after Rhades, a village of the Anatolikon theme.

12. So the emperor sent Eustathios, droungarios of the fleet, against him with the fleet then at hand and the soldiers. They could not draw up to face him and came back empty-handed. When the Hagarenes reached Abydos, they asked the men who were guiding them, "Do we have to go back by this same route, or is there another by which we can get home?" When these answered, "We want to go back by this one," the Hagarenes took fright at the narrowness of the passage. Such are the judgments of God: they turned back at once, [P. 466] fell upon Thessalonica, sacked it, and made great slaughter and took many captives. When they meant to destroy the city as well, Symeon the protoasekretis, who happened to be there, took from Rhodophyllios, who had been sent to the Franks, a basket holding a hundred pounds of gold. He gave both the gold and the basket to the Saracens, and they let the city alone, and the [?]

15. In his nineteenth year Samonas fled toward Syria. Since men were pursuing him from behind, and he had come as far as the Halys, Nikephoros Kaidzes [?], the droungarios, met him and would not let him cross. So he took refuge at the precious cross of Sericha, pretending he had come there to pray. Constantine, son of Doux, took him up and returned with him to the City. The emperor then ordered him to be kept under guard in the house of Bardas the Caesar. Since the emperor wanted to receive Samonas back into his presence, he told Doux not to say before the senate that Samonas had fled to Syria, but that he had gone to Sericha to pray. Then the emperor questioned Constantine before the senate, just as matters stood: "By God and by my head, was Samonas fleeing or not?" When he told the emperor, "He was fleeing," the emperor sent him away in anger. Samonas spent four months and sixteen [days] in the house of Bardas. At that time a comet also appeared, sending out [?] its rays toward the east, and it was visible for forty days and [nights?]. 17. In his twentieth year Samonas was received back into favour at the birth of the emperor's son Constantine, whose mother was Zoe, the emperor's fourth wife. The child was baptized on holy Theophany by Nicholas the patriarch, and Samonas was also made a patrician. 18. In his twenty-first year Leo and Zoe were married after the feast by the priest [?] Thomas, who was later deposed, and Leo proclaimed his wife Augusta. For this the patriarch barred the emperor from entering the church. So he would come in from the right-hand side only as far as the mitatorion, and did not go at all into the places where he usually went. 19. In his twenty-second year the emperor promoted Samonas to parakoimomenos, because he was his accomplice [Note: variant reading "so you have," p. 558 d.]

in every lawless and wicked deed, and they began to scheme against the Church. [P. 467] They summoned Nicholas the patriarch and pressed him hard to accept the fourth marriage. When he would not give way, they put him into a small boat at the Boukoleon and ferried him across to Hiereia. From there he made his way on foot, with great difficulty, as far as Galakrenai, with deep snow lying on the ground. In his place Euthymios the synkellos was ordained patriarch. He was a man of priestly bearing, self-controlled and very devout. It is said that he accepted the fourth marriage because of a divine revelation, since the emperor wanted to introduce a heresy and pass a law allowing a man to have three or four wives, and many very learned men were helping him in this. 20. In the month of June a violent wind [?] blew, so strong that it shook houses and churches. Everyone fled into the open air and said that the end of the world had come. But by the love of God for mankind it was stopped by rain. 21. In the twenty-third year a Saracen fleet set out against the Romans. The emperor appointed Himerios the logothete commander of all the naval forces. He also wrote to Andronikos Doux to join Himerios. But Samonas was implacably hostile to Andronikos and eager to harm him by any means. He persuaded someone to write to him secretly: "Do not go aboard the ships, or you will be arrested by Himerios." Himerios urged Andronikos many times to embark with him while the Hagarenes were pressing hard, but he would not be persuaded.
