So Himerios, on his own, joined battle with the Hagarenes on the day of Saint Thomas and won a great victory. When Andronikos learned of this, he gave up hope. He rebelled together with his kinsmen and his men, went off and seized the city of Kabala, so that Samonas said to the emperor, "Didn't I tell you, master, that Doux was a rebel?" 22. In the twenty-fourth year the emperor sent Gregoras Iberitzes, the domestic of the schools, who was related to Andronikos by marriage, to make war on him. When Andronikos learned this, and heard also that the patriarch had been driven out of the Church, he fled to the Hagarenes with his kinsmen and friends. Leo was grieved at this. He treated a Saracen from the praetorium kindly and sent him to Andronikos with a chrysobull written in cinnabar, [P. 468] which he had placed inside a short candle [?]. When the Saracen had left the emperor's presence, Samonas called him and said, "Do you know what you are carrying?" (meaning the candle) "The ruin of Syria." He gave him money and told him to put it into the hand of the vizier. The man did so. So Andronikos and the men with him were arrested and put in chains. When he learned that this had happened to him through Samonas's treachery, under compulsion

he apostatized. Constantine and the others knew that Andronikos could not possibly get out. Not long afterwards, on his advice, they fled by themselves and, remarkably, made their way out of the heart of Syria into Roman territory, fighting their way through the country. 23. Then old Abelbakes [?] and Samonas's father came from Tarsus to the City to negotiate a settlement. The emperor received them and showed them the treasures of the church. This was unworthy of a Christian state, that godless men should look upon the sacred vessels of God. Samonas's father wanted to stay with his son and not remain in Syria. But Samonas urged him, saying, "Keep your faith. And if I can, I will come to you [?]." 24. In his twenty-fifth year, on the day of Pentecost, Emperor Leo crowned his son Constantine the Porphyrogennetos through the hands of Euthymios the patriarch. Samonas gave his own man Constantine, who had earlier served Basil, the magistros and official in charge of the imperial inkstand, to serve Zoe Augusta. Both Emperor Leo and the Augusta grew very fond of him. As a result Samonas envied him greatly and slandered him, claiming that he was having relations with the Augusta. The emperor suspected this was true and had him tonsured by Samonas in the monastery of Saint Tarasios. A little later he ordered Samonas to take him to the monastery of Ta Speira, because he wished to take him back again. So the emperor went out on a progress to Damatrys, and when he had dined at Samonas's monastery he saw Constantine. At once he gave orders to Samonas, who dressed him in lay clothes; he served wine to the emperor at the banquet, [P. 469] and afterwards returned to the palace. Once again Samonas envied Constantine because of the emperor's love for him. He plotted with Tzirithon and some others, and they produced a pamphlet full of abuse against the emperor, written and composed by Rhodios, Samonas's notary. When the emperor came to the Great Church, Samonas threw it into the mitatorion. The emperor found it, read it, and was in great distress, and searched for whoever had done it. At that time there was an eclipse of the moon, and the emperor ordered the astronomers of the day to say what it portended. As Pantaleon the metropolitan was going in to the emperor, Samonas asked him, "Who is the harm meant for?" He said, "For you. But if the thirteenth of June passes, you will suffer no harm after that." But to the emperor he said that the harm signified by the moon concerned the second man. The emperor took this to mean his brother Alexander. After this Tzirithon told the emperor privately that Samonas had written the paper. At once the emperor removed Samonas from office, sent him down to his house and made him a monk, and then had him taken to the monastery of Euthymios the patriarch. When he was slandered again, they took him to the monastery of Martinakios.

So he removed Samonas from office and made Constantine parakoimomenos. He built him a monastery at Nosiai and went with Euthymios the patriarch to dedicate it. It is worth saying a little about how the monastery of Nosiai came to be built. 25. This Constantine had an aged father, devout and God-fearing. In that very place, Nosiai, he owned a very small suburban estate by the sea, where he had channelled water into a cistern and so gave refreshment to travellers. It happened that a soldier passed by this water. After refreshing himself he took out the coins he had come by honestly and counted them, and they came to three pounds. Then he got up, as people do, mounted his horse and went on his way, leaving the gold where it lay. The old man went out to the cistern as usual, found the gold, and was grieved at the distress of the man who had lost it. He kept it safe with him, and night after night he never stopped praying to God that the man would come back and recover what was his. [P. 470] The soldier, for his part, had passed through the gates before he remembered. Unable to do anything about it, he went on his way grieving. Three years later he came to the place at Nosiai, dismounted, and watered his horse. He drank too, then sat down lost in thought, and with a sigh he said, "In this place I lost my [?]." Hearing this, the venerable old man asked him, "What happened, my lord?" He said, "I lost some coins here." At once he pointed out the spot and described the marks on the purse and how much was in it. Immediately the man of God drew it out of the fold of his garment and said, "Do you recognize this?" The soldier was [?] and held speechless for a long while, but at last he said, "Yes, this is what I lost." The old man said, "Take it back, and rest assured that I have not opened it or looked at what is inside." The man took it and begged him to take as much of it as he liked. But he would not take anything at all. So the soldier went on his way, rejoicing and giving thanks to God. That night the old man saw in a dream [?] coming to him and saying, "Because you have acted in this way toward the soldier, tomorrow you will hear that your son has been made parakoimomenos. This estate of yours will become a great monastery to glorify me, and you yourself will receive the reward for these deeds." In the morning the message came. A few days later, by the emperor's will and at his expense, as has been said, the monastery was built and dedicated. 26. In the same year a naval war with the Saracens was fought for eight months by Himerios the logothete, while Romanos, who later became emperor, was strategos at Samos. There was a defeat: [Variant readings: "this" for "it"; "was begging" in the margin.]

Himerios was beaten and barely escaped, and almost everyone there was in danger. After this Emperor Leo fell ill with a disease of the bowels. There was also a fire at the candle workshops of the Great Church, and all the archives and the sakelle were burned. On the eleventh of May Emperor Leo died, having appointed his brother Alexander emperor. They say that when he saw him coming in to him he said, "Here comes the bad time, after thirteen months," and begged him earnestly to protect his son Constantine. Emperor of the Romans: Alexander, with Constantine the Porphyrogennetos, one year and [?] days. [P. 471] Year of the world 6420 [?], of the divine incarnation 920 [?]. Emperor of the Romans: Alexander, with Constantine the Porphyrogennetos, son of Leo, one year and [?] days. Alexander at once sent for Nicholas, brought him back from Galakrenai, and enthroned him. He removed Euthymios and exiled him to the monastery of Agathou. A few days later he brought him to the Magnaura, and there they held a silention and a synod and deposed him. They shamefully plucked out the beard of that priestly and admirable man and heaped other insults and punishments on him, all of which this holy shepherd bore quietly and meekly. Then he was sent back to Agathou, where he died. He was buried in his own monastery in the City, at Ta Psamathiou. As for the cleric who plucked out the patriarch's hair, at the very hour the saint was sent into exile his house was burned by an invisible fire. His daughter was struck by complete paralysis. She could not move her hand or mouth or any other part of her body, nor utter a sound, and she lived on, bedridden and begging, until the reign of Emperor Nikephoros, son of Niketas. Emperor Alexander was incapable of doing any work befitting an emperor and spent all his time hunting and on wicked pursuits. Several times he wanted to castrate Leo's son, but he was talked out of it by those whom Leo had treated well, who pleaded sometimes that the boy was an infant, sometimes that he was sickly. In his reign a comet appeared in the west for forty days. People said it was a "swordfish" and signified that bloodshed would take place in the City. This Alexander gave himself over to deceivers and sorcerers. They told him, and he believed it, that his life was bound up with the talisman of the wild boar in the Hippodrome, [P. 472] hinting in this way at his swinish and senseless way of life. Persuaded by them, he fitted the boar with genitals and teeth, on the grounds that it lacked them. Trusting in their deception, he decorated the Hippodrome and held an illumination in honour of the statue. For this the hand of Christ was withdrawn from him, since he had given the honour due to God to idols. 2. Himerios, however, [on his return?] from the Hagarenes'

[?] with [blood?] flowing from his genitals, he died two days later. He left Nicholas the patriarch, Stephen the magistros, and John Eladas the rhaiktor as guardians, and the empire to Constantine, son of Leo. After his death he was buried with his father Basil. Emperor of the Romans: Constantine the Porphyrogennetos, forty-eight years. Year of the world 6421 [?], of the divine incarnation 921 [?]. Emperor of the Romans: Constantine the Porphyrogennetos, forty-eight years. When his father Leo died he was seven years old, and his uncle Alexander left him under guardians. He reigned under these same guardians together with his mother for seven years. Alongside his father-in-law Romanos, in a subordinate position, he reigned twenty-six years, and as sole ruler fifteen years, so that the whole length of his reign was forty-eight years. Patriarch Nicholas took control of the palace, since he too was a guardian, [P. 473] and together with the magistroi Stephen and John Eladas he managed public affairs and had full charge of all matters concerning the empire.

2. While the government was in this state, some of the magnates in the City sent word to Constantine Doux, who was domestic of the schools. They admired him as brave and sensible and well able to govern the empire, and they urged him to come in and make himself master of it without any trouble. He had long desired it. As fast as he could, he reached the imperial city with picked men from the army under his command, a sufficient number of them. He entered by night through the postern of the protovestiarios Melana [?], which is near the acropolis, and spent the night without sleep, together with his companions, in the house of his father-in-law Gregoras. But Niketas the asekretis, who later became protonotarios, reported Constantine's arrival to Constantine Eladikos, patrician and monk. That same night both of them came to Constantine Doux. At dawn, before day had broken and while it was still dark, with torches, a large crowd and weapons,

they seized the gate of the Hippodrome and acclaimed Constantine emperor in the Hippodrome. There his groom was speared and killed by the men inside the Hippodrome gates. Constantine was not let in there but was driven off. As though driven mad by some demon, his reason unsettled by his lust for the throne, he withdrew from the Hippodrome gloomy and downcast, judging the killing of his groom an evil omen. From there he went to the Chalke, entered through the Iron Gate of the Chalke, and came as far as the Excubita. John Eladas the magistros picked men from the hetaireia and others and sent them armed against Doux. When they reached the Chalke, many fell on both sides, so many that the place was flooded with blood. Gregoras, Doux's son, was killed, along with his cousin Michael and the well-known Kourtikes the Armenian. When Constantine Doux learned this, [P. 474] since the confusion was very great, he spurred on his horse. But the horse slipped on the paving slabs there and threw its rider to the ground, and someone cut off his head with a sword. It was brought to the emperor, making plain to everyone [?] the deceit.

3. His attempt had also been revealed in another way. A certain Nicholas, who had been entrusted with the collection of public taxes in Chaldia, went over to Syria, renounced our faith, and turned instead to astrology, or some kind of astronomy. He wrote on a cloth dyed black and sent it to Thomas the logothete. When Manuel, the interpreter for the Hagarenes, dropped it into water, the letters written on it became visible. They said: "Do not fear the red cock, Doux. He will rebel foolishly and be destroyed at once." 4. When this was over, Gregoras, his father-in-law, together with Leo, whom they called Choirosphaktes, took refuge in the church of the Holy Wisdom of God. They dragged them out of it by force and tonsured them in the monastery of Stoudios. Constantine Eladikos they flogged with ox-hide whips, paraded him on a donkey in a coarse robe [?], and shut him up in the prison of the Dalmatoi. Others they blinded and exiled, and others they beheaded. The men of the army, who were brave, fine and numerous, they impaled, every one of them, all the way from Damalis to Leukaton. The so-called guardians would have destroyed many others too, had not some of the judges checked them in their unjust fury, saying, "The emperor is a child. How dare you do such things without his command?"

They tonsured Doux's wife, castrated his son, and sent them off to their house in Paphlagonia. 5. In the month of August Symeon the Bulgarian reached Constantinople with a huge host and built a palisade around it from sea to sea, buoyed up by high hopes. But he was disappointed in his hopes because of [?] his host and the strength of the defenders' weapons and walls. He withdrew to the Hebdomon and asked for a peace treaty. The guardians very gladly accepted peace, and Symeon and his sons, honoured with vast and splendid gifts, returned to their own country. [P. 475] 6. Emperor Constantine was a child and kept asking for his mother, for Alexander had already put her out of the palace. So they brought her back. Once she had taken full control of the government, she brought Constantine the parakoimomenos back to the palace, along with Constantine and Anastasios Gongylios. On the advice of John Eladas she removed the household of Emperor Alexander, that is, John the rhaiktor, Gabrielopoulos and the rest. Zoe Augusta appointed Theophylaktos, son of Dominikos, as hetaireiarches. John Eladas the magistros fell ill and died. On the advice of Theophylaktos the hetaireiarches, Zoe angrily put Nicholas the patriarch out of the palace, telling him to look after his own church and take care of it. Not long afterwards Constantine the parakoimomenos denounced the hetaireiarches to Zoe, claiming that he was trying to seize the throne for his brother. So on a pretext they made him a patrician, and when he went down to the church, as was the custom, to receive a blessing, she ordered him to stay at home. Zoe then appointed John Garidas hetaireiarches, and Damian droungarios of the Watch.

7. While Symeon the Bulgarian was plundering Thrace, John Bogas asked to be made [strategos?] and to bring the Pechenegs against him. He received gifts and set out, and he brought hostages back to the City, after the Pechenegs had agreed to cross over and make war on Symeon. 8. Asotios also came to the City. He was a man [?] who was famous for his strength, the son of the archon of archons. It is said that he could take an iron bar in his hands by both ends and, with his extraordinary strength, bend it into the shape of a circle, the stubborn nature of the iron yielding to the force of his hands. When he arrived they received him with great honour and then sent him back to his own country. 9. In the month of September, in the third indiction, Pankratoukas the Armenian betrayed Adrianople to Symeon. Not long afterwards Basil the patrician was sent with many gifts, and

[?] it. Damian the emir also came with a fleet to Strobilos, and he would have taken it had he not fallen ill and died, and the Saracens turned back with nothing to show for it. The inhabitants of Hellas and Athens had suffered constant abuse from Chases, the son of Iouvi [?]. Unable to bear his profligacy and greed any longer, they stoned him to death inside the church at Athens.

10. Zoe saw how arrogantly Symeon was acting against the Christians. She resolved with those in high office to arrange an exchange of prisoners and a peace with the Hagarenes, and to bring the whole army of the East across to make war on Symeon. So John Rhadenos the patrician and Michael Toxaras were sent to Syria to make the exchange. After lavishing gifts on all the themes, she brought them across to Thrace. Leo Phokas the magistros was domestic at the time, a man endowed more with courage than with the judgment needed for command. The generals and commanders, binding themselves fast in concord with one another, swore an oath on the precious wood of the Cross, and once the oath was taken they set out with the whole army. John Grapson commanded the tagma of the Exkoubitoi, and the son of Maroules that of the Hikanatoi. Romanos Argyros was a general, as were Leo his brother and Bardas Phokas, and Melias was with them with the Armenians. Constantine Lips the patrician was also there, acting as Leo's [?] adviser in all that concerned him. On 20 August, in the fifth indiction, battle was joined between the Bulgarians and the Romans by the river Achelous. Such are the judgments of God: a slaughter took place such as had never happened since time began. Leo the Doux [?] fled and escaped to Mesembria. Among others killed in the clash of battle were Constantine Lips, John Grapson and many other commanders. Romanos, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, had been sent with the whole fleet into the river Danube to help Leo Phokas. John Bogas had also been sent to bring down the Pechenegs, as was said before, and the droungarios Romanos had been ordered to ferry them across. But the two fell to quarrelling, and when the Pechenegs saw them at odds, they withdrew to their own lands. When the war was over and Romanos and Bogas had returned to the City, the City turned against them. They put the droungarios Romanos in such danger that he was sentenced to be blinded, on the grounds that through negligence, or rather malice, he had failed to ferry the Pechenegs across and had not taken the fleeing Romans aboard his ships. He would have suffered this too, had the sentence not been overturned by Constantine Gongyles the patrician and Stephen the magistros, who had great influence with the Augusta.

11. When the Bulgarians marched as far as the City, Leo, the domestic of the Scholai, went out

together with Nicholas his son and John the hetaireiarch, with a very large force, to Katasyrtai. The Bulgarians fell on them unexpectedly in the night, and they all perished utterly.

12. Theodore, the tutor of the emperor Constantine, saw that Constantine the parakoimomenos was scheming to secure the throne for his own brother-in-law Leo. He therefore advised the emperor Constantine to take on Romanos the droungarios, who had been his father's servant and was loyal to him, so that with Romanos at his side he might be protected and have an ally and helper whenever he needed one. Romanos had often been approached about this and had refused. So the emperor Constantine wrote a note in his own hand and sent it to Romanos, directed against the parakoimomenos. As the rumour of this spread, the parakoimomenos kept pressing Romanos to set out with the fleet, but Romanos made the excuse that he could not sail, since the fleet had not received its customary pay. Constantine the parakoimomenos, pressing him hard, went out to the dockyard. Romanos met him with the bearing of a servant, and when he came close he seized him. "Take him away!" he shouted, and his men carried him into the trireme of the droungarios Romanos and held him under guard. The emperor Constantine was now drawing power away from his mother to himself, and the next day he sent John Toubakes to bring the Augusta Zoe down from the palace. With wailing and tears she clung to her son and moved him to pity and a son's compassion for his mother. "Let my mother stay with me," he said, and at his word they let her go. On the patriarch's advice, the emperor appointed John Garidas domestic of the Scholai, for he feared that Leo Phokas would rebel. He would not consent to this unless they appointed his brother-in-law Theodore Zouphinezer and his son Symeon as hetaireiarchs. He went out at once to Romanos, and after oaths were given and received, he came to be of one mind and one spirit with him.

13. On 24 March Romanos sent a message to the palace to explain himself: "I feared an attack by Phokas and some revolt against the emperor, and I did this in order to guard the emperor." He was then told to come with the whole fleet as far as the Boukoleon. On the day of the [?] (it was a Thursday), he came armed into the Boukoleon with the whole fleet. Stephen the patrician left the palace at once, and Niketas, Romanos' co-father-in-law, went up into the palace and brought the patriarch Nicholas out of it. Once Romanos had assured them under oath, the people of the palace sent him the precious and life-giving [?] Cross. He venerated it and confirmed them by oath [?], and then went up with them and a few [?]

to the palace. He did obeisance to the emperor, went with him into the church of the Pharos and gave him pledges of loyalty, and he was immediately appointed magistros and great hetaireiarch. At once an order was sent to Leo Phokas instructing him on no account to contemplate any sedition, but to rest for a while in his own house. Constantine the parakoimomenos was likewise ordered to write him a letter with the same instructions, telling him to remain in submission to the emperor Constantine. Leo received these from Andrew, the primikerios of the imperial protovestiarios [?], and kept quiet at his own house in Cappadocia. So the oracle in verse was fulfilled: "[?] then the nightingale [?], leading it to a desert island [?], to become prey and spoil for the birds; but the eagle, though willing [?], [?] home."

14. In the month of April the emperor Constantine gave a pledge of marriage to Helena, the daughter of Romanos, and on the third day of Galilee week they were crowned in marriage by the patriarch Nicholas. The emperor named Romanos basileopator and made his son Christopher hetaireiarch in his place. Not long afterwards Leo Phokas was led astray by certain officials and moved towards rebellion. He sent for Constantine the parakoimomenos and Constantine the asekretis, the son of Malelias, and took them to be with him, assuring everyone and insisting that he was mounting this uprising on behalf of the emperor Constantine. Romanos the basileopator then issued a signed chrysobull in the name of the emperor Constantine, meant to defeat this plot. It declared: "All who abandon Phokas and take refuge with the basileopator are on the emperor's side." He gave it to a shameless and bold woman named Anna, whom they also called Basian [?], and to a cleric named Michael, and sent them into the camp, where they spread it throughout the army. Michael was caught, beaten without mercy, and had his nose and ears cut off, but afterwards Romanos gave him a fitting reward, and likewise Anna, the woman who had been sent with him. The first to abandon Phokas and run over to Romanos was Constantine, the son of Barymichael, commander of the tagma of the Hikanatoi, and this was the beginning of Phokas' downfall. With him went Balantios and the man called Atzmoros, both of them tourmarchs. Leo Phokas occupied Chrysopolis with a very large force. The city is called Chrysopolis after Alexander. When he came to the city of Byzas, he encamped his army at a certain spot in it, and so the enclosure he put up was named the Strategion. Then he moved on, crossed to the opposite shore, and gave his army a large amount of gold. Others say it was named for the gold that came

from its mines, just as Chalcedon got its name from having copper, or else from Chalcis, the daughter of Nicomedes, who founded it. In this same Chrysopolis there died the wife of Chares the Athenian general, whose name was Damalis, at the time when Chares had been sent from Athens to help the Byzantines. Above her tomb a heifer (damalis), named after her, was set up on a column, and an epigram was composed for it, which runs as follows:
"I am not the image of Inachus' cow, nor is the Bosporan sea before me named for me. Long ago Hera's heavy wrath drove her to Pharos; but I am a Cecropian corpse [?] of Athens. [?] here [?] the enemy's ships [?]. Then I was called Boidion; but now, as the wife of Chares, I delight in both continents [?]."

15. Having occupied Chrysopolis, as was said, Phokas drew up his battle lines from Damalis to Chalcedon to frighten the people in the City. Romanos sent Symeon, the official in charge of the imperial inkstand, in a dromon, carrying a signed document of the emperor Constantine: "I have found none of my subjects to be a more vigilant, loyal and faithful guardian of my majesty than Romanos, and so, after God, I have entrusted my protection to him. I have decided to regard him as a father, since he has shown me a father's tenderness and a parent's affection. As for this Leo Phokas, I always suspected him of plotting against my majesty, and now I have found him by his very deeds to be a plotter, rising up like a usurper against my rule. Therefore I do not wish him to be domestic from now on. Nor do I say that he carried out this rebellion with my approval. He made this attack of his own free choice, to seize the throne for himself." When this was read out to the army, everyone began to withdraw and stream over to Romanos the basileopator. Phokas found himself at a loss and fled to Aetoi, but he was not received there. He reached a village called Goeleon [?] and was seized there, and Romanos sent John Toubakes and his own kinsman Leo to bring him back. They blinded him against Romanos' wishes.

16. In the month of August a plot was denounced, devised by Constantine Ktematerou [?], David Kamoulianos and Michael, kouropalatai of the Mangana [?]. They were beaten, hunted down and paraded, and then sent into exile. The Augusta too was caught plotting against Romanos with poisoned food. They brought her down from the palace and tonsured her in the monastery of St Euphemia. Theophylact [?] invited

Theodore, the tutor of the emperor Constantine, and his brother Symeon, and while they were eating, John Kourkouas, droungarios of the Watch, came in with a large body of men. He seized them on the grounds that they were plotting against Romanos and exiled them to the Opsikion.

17. On 24 September Romanos was honoured with the rank of Caesar, and on 17 December he was crowned by the emperor Constantine and the patriarch Nicholas, in the year 6428, in the eighth indiction. At the holy Theophany his wife Theodora was crowned. On the same day of the same month in the fifth [?] indiction, Christopher, the son of Romanos, was proclaimed emperor. He was crowned at Pentecost by the emperor Constantine [?], and these two alone went forth in the procession.

18. In the month of July of the same indiction the union of the schismatics took place.

19. In the month of October of the ninth indiction, Stephen the magistros was suspected of aspiring to the throne and was tonsured on the island of Antigonos, together with his men Theophanes Teicheotes and Paul the orphanotrophos. Again a plot was denounced, devised by Arsenios and Paul, the manglabitai. They were beaten, their property was confiscated, and they were exiled [?].

20. Rentakes the Helladic had become a parricide. He plundered all his father's property and fled to the City, and from there, after forging false letters, he was about to escape to Bulgaria. He was caught, and his eyes were gouged out.

21. After the death of the Doux Adralestos the Bulgarians again advanced as far as Katasyrtai. Pothos, the son of Argyros, was appointed domestic of the Scholai. He came as far as Thermopolis with the tagmata and sent Michael, the son of Moroleon, to spy on the Bulgarians. Michael stumbled unawares on their ambush and killed many of the Bulgarians, but he was wounded himself, and after making his way into the City he died.

22. Again a plot against Romanos was denounced, to be carried out by Anastasios the sakellarios, Theodoretos the koitonites of the eidikon and some others, who claimed to be fighting on behalf of the emperor Constantine. They were convicted, beaten, paraded through the Mese and sent into exile.

23. Seizing on this pretext, Romanos demoted the emperor Constantine and made him second to himself. The Bulgarians again campaigned as far as the Manglabas [?]. When the emperor Romanos learned of this, he sent John the rhaiktor with Leo and Pothos, the Argyroi, who had with them a sizeable force drawn from the tagmata and

from the hetaireia. With them also was Alexios Mousele, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, with his men. They drew up their forces on the plain and the low-lying ground of Pegai. The Bulgarians appeared above them in arms, raised a wordless and terrifying shout, and charged at them with the utmost violence. The rhaiktor fled at once. Photeinos, the son of Platypous, was killed fighting to defend him. Of the rest, some were slaughtered, some perished in the sea, and others were taken captive. The Argyroi fled into the fort and were saved. With no one to stop them, the Bulgarians set fire to the palaces of Pegai and burned the whole Stenon.

24. In the month of February, in the tenth indiction,

25. Again, in the month of June, the Bulgarians came as far as the palaces of St Theodora. They set these on fire and plundered everything that lay beyond. Again there was a battle, and the Romans were routed. The man called Saktikes performed many brave deeds and killed many, but he could not hold out against the multitude. He fled with a mortal wound, was laid in the church of Blachernae and died soon after.

26. A rebellion broke out in Chaldia, led by Adrian the Chaldian and Tatzates the Armenian at the instigation of Bardas Boilas, who was general in Chaldia, and the fortress of Paiperte was seized. John Kourkouas, the domestic of the Scholai, defeated and captured them. He blinded the more prominent of them and confiscated their property, but the poor and obscure he ordered to go free and unharmed wherever they wished. Tatzates escaped to another fortress, asked for a guarantee of safety and came into the City. He was made a magistros and lived under guard in the Mangana. When he planned to escape he was caught and deprived of his eyes. Bardas Boilas they tonsured, because the emperor took pity on him.

27. Symeon laid siege to Adrianople with his whole army and pressed the siege hard. A severe famine was crushing the inhabitants, and they had nowhere to get provisions, so they surrendered themselves and their general to the Bulgarians. The general was the son of Moroleon, or rather Thymoleon, to give him a more fitting name, a man excellent in every respect and famous in war, who had performed a great many

brave deeds against the Bulgarians. Symeon took him prisoner, punished him with countless tortures and at last killed him. Then he handed the city over to the Bulgarians to guard and withdrew. When they heard that the Romans were marching against them, they abandoned the city and left, and it came under the Romans once more.

28. Leo of Tripoli arrived at the island of Lemnos with a great force. John Rhadenos, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, fell on them suddenly and destroyed them all, and only Leo of Tripoli himself escaped.

29. In the month of September of the second indiction, Symeon the Bulgarian again marched against Constantinople with his whole army. He plundered Thrace and Macedonia, burning and destroying everything and cutting down the trees, and came as far as Blachernae. He then asked for the patriarch Nicholas and some of the magnates to be sent to him, so that they could talk with him about peace. Both sides took hostages, and the patriarch went out, with Michael Stypiotes the patrician and John the mystikos, who was then the most powerful man at court; for John the rhaiktor had already been slandered to the emperor and tonsured. They discussed peace with Symeon, but he wanted to see the emperor Romanos himself. When the emperor heard this he was overjoyed, for he longed for peace and an end to the shedding of blood. He sent men to the shore at Kosmidion and had a very strong landing stage built out into the sea, so that the imperial trireme could sail in and moor there. He had it fenced in on every side and ordered a dividing wall built across the middle, where they were to talk with each other. Meanwhile Symeon sent men to set fire to the church of the most holy Theotokos at Pege, which the emperor Justinian had built, together with everything around it. This made it plain that he did not want peace but was deceiving the emperor with empty hopes. The emperor came with the patriarch to Blachernae and went into the holy reliquary chapel. He stretched out his hands in prayer, then fell on his face and wet the holy floor with his tears, beseeching the all-immaculate Theotokos to soften the unbending and implacable heart of proud Symeon and persuade him to agree to peace. Then he took the holy veil of the all-holy Theotokos from its chest, left the church, and went to the appointed place. It was 9 September, a Thursday. At the fourth hour Symeon arrived, bringing a countless host divided into many battalions. Some carried gold shields and gold spears, others silver shields and silver spears, and others were decked out in arms of every colour, all of them clad in iron. They had Symeon in their midst and acclaimed him as emperor in the language of the Romans. All

the members of the senate stood on the walls and watched what was happening. Then one could see a truly imperial and noble soul, and marvel at his unshakable spirit and courageous bearing. Seeing such a mass of enemies bearing down, he was not dismayed, did not shrink back and did not retreat. He went forward as calmly as if he were walking into a crowd of friends, all but offering up his own life to the enemy as a ransom for his subjects. He reached the landing stage first and waited for Symeon. Hostages were taken on both sides, and the Bulgarians searched the landing stage thoroughly in case there was some trick or ambush. Then Symeon got off his horse and went in to the emperor. They greeted each other and began to speak of peace. The emperor is said to have spoken to Symeon as follows:
"I have heard that you are a God-fearing man and a true Christian, but I see that your deeds do not match your words at all. It is the mark of a God-fearing man and a Christian to embrace peace and love, since God is love, as it is said. It is the mark of an impious man and an unbeliever to delight in slaughter and in blood unjustly shed. If, then, you are a true Christian, as we have been assured, put a stop at last to these unjust slaughters and this unholy bloodshed, and make peace with us Christians, since you are yourself a Christian and bear the name. Do not choose to stain Christian hands with the blood of fellow believers. You too are a man, awaiting death, resurrection, judgment and recompense, here today and tomorrow turned to dust. A single fever will snuff out all your arrogance. What account will you give to God, when you go from here, for these unjust slaughters? With what face will you look upon that fearsome and just Judge? If you love wealth [?], I will fill you with it till you have more than enough. Only hold back your hand, embrace peace and cherish concord, so that you may live a peaceful, bloodless and untroubled life yourself, and the Christians may at last be freed from their calamities and stop killing Christians. For it is not right for them to take up arms against their fellow believers."

30. When the emperor had said this much he fell silent. Symeon was abashed by such humility and by his words, and he agreed to make peace. They greeted each other and parted, after the emperor had honoured Symeon with magnificent gifts. I will now tell what happened at that moment, a portent and a marvel to those who know how to interpret such things. They say that while the emperors were talking, two eagles flew above them, screeched, came together, and then at once separated, one going towards the City and the other towards Thrace.

[?] …to fly across. Those who study such things carefully judged this a bad omen, for they said that the two would part without coming to terms on the peace. Symeon, on reaching his own camp, told his magnates of the emperor's intelligence and humility, and praised to the skies his appearance, his strength and the undaunted firmness of his spirit. 31. On 25 December Romanos crowned his sons Stephen and Constantine in the Great Church. His son Theophylact, who was a eunuch, the patriarch Nicholas made a cleric; he appointed him synkellos and ordained him subdeacon. On 15 May, in the third indiction, the patriarch Nicholas died, having held the patriarchate for thirteen years in his second tenure, and he was buried in his monastery of Galakrenai. In August Stephen of Amaseia, a eunuch, became patriarch. John the mystikos, who was the chief minister, was convicted of plotting against the emperor; he fled and was tonsured in the monastery of Monokastanos. Constantine, son of Boilas, was tonsured on Olympus. The emperor Romanos then appointed Theophanes the protovestiarios as chief minister. At that time there was a terrible earthquake in the Thrakesion theme, and a great and frightful chasm opened in the earth, so that many villages and churches were swallowed up together with their inhabitants.

33. On 27 May, in the fifteenth indiction, John the astronomer said to the emperor Romanos: "The statue that stands on top of the arch of the Xerolophos and faces west is Symeon's. If you cut off its head, Symeon will die in that same hour." So the emperor sent men by night and had the head of the statue cut off, and in that same hour Symeon died in Bulgaria. He had appointed as ruler his son Peter, whom he had by his second wife, and had had Michael, his son by his first wife, tonsured a monk. John and Benjamin, Peter's brothers, still wore Bulgarian dress. 34. When the surrounding nations, the Croats and the rest, learned of Symeon's death, they wanted to move against the Bulgarians. A very great famine, together with locusts, was afflicting Bulgaria, and the Bulgarians feared a Roman attack even more. So they marched against Roman territory and ravaged Macedonia. But when the Bulgarians heard that the emperor was setting out against them, they turned their minds to peace and sent a monk named Kalokyres, an Armenian by race. The emperor received him most gladly, and he [?]

confirmed the peace, and asked to make a marriage alliance with the emperor. They made an agreement to give Peter Maria, daughter of the emperor Christopher, and wrote to Peter to come. [?] So the magistros Niketas, father-in-law of the emperor Romanos's son, was sent to meet him and bring him to the city. When they arrived at Blachernai, the emperor went out and embraced him. After they had talked as was fitting, they signed the peace treaty and the marriage contracts, with the protovestiarios Theophanes acting as mediator. On 8 October Peter and Maria were crowned in the church of the most holy Theotokos of the Pege by the patriarch Stephen. When all the customary ceremonies had been splendidly performed, the Bulgarians insisted strongly that Christopher be acclaimed first, and then Constantine, and the emperor agreed to this. A few days later Peter took his wife Maria and set off for Bulgaria. 35. Envoys came from Melitene, and with them their general Apolasath. Romanos received them with fitting honour, and after making a peace treaty they returned home. From then on they campaigned with the Romans against their fellow Saracens, and they joined the Romans in the triumphal processions in the city, leading Hagarene captives. This was a marvellous and extraordinary thing, and a sign of the misfortune of the godless Hagarenes. But when Apolasath, a prudent and intelligent man, died, the inhabitants of Melitene broke the peace. So the Domestic of the Scholai, John Kourkouas, marched against them with the themes and the tagmata, along with Melias and the Armenians. They reduced Melitene and its surroundings to such straits that the emperor made it a crown estate and drew many thousands in gold and silver from it each year. 36. The magistros Niketas, father-in-law of the emperor Christopher, was accused of urging Christopher to turn against his own father and drive him from the throne. They banished him from the city and made him a monk. 37. On 18 June, in the sixth indiction, the patriarch Stephen died, having held office for two years and eleven months. On 14 December they brought Tryphon from the Opsikion, a man attested for his piety and holiness, and ordained him patriarch for a fixed term. But he would not accept being patriarch for a fixed term, only until the end of his life, so they won him over by a trick, as follows. Since he would not agree, they said: "This man does not know his letters and cannot write, and that is why he is resisting." Wanting to prove to them that he could both write and read, he asked for

paper and ink. They gave him a fresh roll and had him write somewhere down at the bottom: "Tryphon, by the mercy of God monk and patriarch, being satisfied with and assenting to what is written above, I have signed with my own hand." Taking this, they ordained him patriarch. Then above the signature of the patriarch Tryphon they wrote whatever they wished, and when the fixed term was complete they deposed him against his will. Yet he was bound by his own signature, though he could not bear the deceit. This was done because Theophylact, son of the emperor Romanos, was by now coming of age. 38. On the 25th of the same month an unbearable winter set in, so that the earth was frozen for 120 days. As a result there was a great famine, and from it great mortality, so that the living could not carry out the dead. The emperor Romanos, seeing the unbearable violence of the cold and seeking to relieve the want caused by the famine, closed off the porticoes of the colonnades with shutters and boards, so that the snow and the cold could not get in at the poor there, and he set up shelters in all the colonnades. He ordered money to be given every month to the poor who lay in them, and the monthly and quarterly allowances to be distributed to the poor in the churches, so that the sum given each month came to twelve thousand in coined silver. Three poor men ate with him every day, each receiving one nomisma; on Wednesdays and Fridays monks did the same, each also receiving one nomisma. One of the boys read aloud at his table. He was as great a lover of monks as anyone, and he told his deeds with tears to all monks who devoted themselves to virtue. He adorned the churches in every way, sent stipends to the monks on all the holy mountains, cared for the monasteries, and never stopped paying the stipends he had fixed for those tonsured in them for God's sake or living as recluses. These few out of the many, of his countless good works and almsgivings, we have related. 39. John, brother of Peter the Bulgarian, together with other magnates of Symeon, plotted against Peter. They were found out: John was beaten and shut up in prison, and the rest were subjected to extraordinary punishments. When the emperor learned of this, he sent and took John to himself. 40. On 2 March a cornice fell in the Forum from the columns standing in a row there and killed six men. There was also a fire in the colonnade of the most holy Theotokos of the Forum, and the wax-chandlers' and furriers' shops burned as far as the Psichai. 41. In August, in the fourth indiction,

the emperor Christopher died and was buried in his father's house. They also deposed the patriarch Tryphon once he had completed the fixed term, and he died in his own monastery. The Church was without a patriarch for one year and five months, because Theophylact, son of [?]

42. A certain Basil, a Macedonian impostor, claimed to be Constantine Doukas and drew many people after him. He was arrested and lost one of his hands. Then, seizing an opportunity, he went back to the Opsikion. He fitted a bronze hand in place of the one that had been cut off, had a huge sword made, and went about deceiving many into believing that he was Constantine Doukas. He seized a fortress called Plateia Petra and a great store of food [?]

44. In April, in the seventh indiction, the Turks made their first campaign against Roman territory. They raided as far as the city and carried off every soul in Thrace. [?] Theophanes the protovestiarios [?] and made a settlement with them. 45. On 14 January Romanos took a wife for his youngest son Constantine. She was of Armeniac stock, named Helen, the daughter of the patrician Adrian. When she died in February, he joined him to another wife, named Theophano, of the family of the [?]. 46. In that year the Rus, also called Dromitai, who are of the race of the Franks, sailed down against Constantinople with [?] ships [?]

[?] attacked them and burned most of their ships, and the rest turned to flight. So the rout became complete: some of their ships were sunk with all hands, and very many men were captured alive. The survivors sailed across to the eastern side, to the place called Rhogai. When they sent a detachment into the regions of Bithynia for supplies, Bardas Phokas came upon them, for he had been sent for this purpose with picked horsemen, and he rode them down and slaughtered them all. Kourkouas also came down with the whole army of the East, and whoever was left he found and killed. The Rus had burned many places and churches. Of the Romans they captured, some they crucified, others they pinned to the ground, and members of the clergy they bound with their hands behind them and drove iron nails through the middle of their heads. As winter was now setting in and they wanted to go home, they tried to slip past the fleet. But when they sailed out by night, the patrician Theophanes met them. At once a second sea battle was joined, and a great many ships were sunk. A few ships escaped and ran ashore on the coast of Koile, and when night came on they fled. Theophanes returned with a great victory and was received by the emperor with honour and magnificence, and he was honoured with the rank of parakoimomenos. 47. In April, in the first indiction, the Turks came again with a very large force. The parakoimomenos went out and concluded a peace treaty with them, so that the peace was for four years [?]

48. In the second indiction Paschalios, protospatharios and strategos of Longobardia, was sent to the king of the Franks to bring back his daughter as a bride for Romanos, son of Constantine, the emperor's son-in-law. Paschalios brought her back with much wealth, and the wedding took place in September, in the third indiction. She lived with her husband for five years and died in the days of the sole reign of Constantine, her father-in-law. 49. In December, in the fourth indiction, a violent and powerful wind blew, and the figures in the Hippodrome called the Demes, opposite the imperial throne, fell down and smashed the benches and parapets beneath them. Some time later, in the same month, the emperor Romanos's sons brought him down from the palace. 50. The city of Edessa, where the holy imprint of Christ was kept, was being besieged by the Roman army, and its inhabitants sent envoys to the emperor Romanos offering to hand it over if he lifted the siege. And this

was done. A chrysobull was given that their country would no longer be plundered by the Romans. When the holy imprint was sent, the parakoimomenos Theophanes met it at the river Sangarios with a brilliant display of lights and with due honour and hymns. On the 19th of the same month he entered the city with it. The emperor was at Blachernai and venerated it there. The next day the emperor's two sons, Stephen and Constantine, and his son-in-law Constantine, together with the patriarch Theophylact and the whole senate, came to the Golden Gate. With the people going before them carrying lights, they bore it on foot to the church of God's Holy Wisdom, and after it had been venerated there they took it up into the palace. 51. In those days an Armenian prodigy visited the city: twin boys, joined together, born from one womb. They were complete in all the limbs of the body, but they were joined to each other face to face from the pit of the stomach down to the lower belly. They spent a long time in the city and were marvelled at by everyone as an extraordinary prodigy; for that very reason they were driven out of the city as an evil omen. They came back again during the sole reign of Constantine. Since one of them had died, some skilled doctors deftly cut through the joined part in the hope that the other would live. But he too survived only three days and died. 52. In everything, as was said above, the emperor had boundless faith in monks, but above all he honoured and revered Sergios, who shone among the monks. He was the brother of the magistros Thomas and the nephew of the patriarch Photios. He was honoured less for his noble birth in the flesh than for the nobility of his soul: the soundness of his judgement, the grace of his face, and the moderation of his mind and character. His speech dripped sweeter than honey, his character was firm and steady, and his mind was wholly unaffected and humble. The emperor kept this celebrated man always by his side, as a rule, one might say, constantly regulating his life. He often urged the emperor to look after his sons and not leave them undisciplined and inclined to wickedness, lest he suffer the fate of Eli and pay the penalty for his sons' lawlessness. And that is what happened. A few days before these events, when everyone was looking at the undefiled likeness of the Son of God on the holy imprint, the emperor's sons said that they saw nothing but a face, while his son-in-law Constantine said that he saw eyes and ears. To them the

celebrated Sergios said: "You have both spoken well." They replied: "And what does the difference between each of these mean?" He answered: "It is not I but David the prophet who says: 'The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.'" When they heard this they were filled with anger and plotted against him. For this reason they brought their father down from the palace and exiled him to the island. But there too the emperor Romanos had Sergios as his consolation in misfortune and a healing medicine for his afflictions. With him was also Polyeuktos, a most pious monk, who consoled him as was fitting. When the patriarch Theophylact died, Polyeuktos was himself appointed patriarch of Constantinople by the emperor Constantine. He too had been introduced to the emperor Romanos by Sergios, the most pious monk already mentioned, in the following way. Since the patriarch Theophylact, Romanos's son, was frequently ill, Romanos urged Sergios to become patriarch. Sergios refused with all his heart, though he was pressed for many days. At last he said: "Master, if you wish, I will bring you a man for patriarch who is pious and capable, and wise as well, fit for such an office." The emperor said: "Let me see him." Polyeuktos came with Sergios, and when they had both come in to the emperor, the emperor sat on his couch and Sergios sat beside him, but they seated Polyeuktos on a stool. The emperor asked Polyeuktos some useful point of Scripture, intending to hear something of how he spoke, as people do. But Polyeuktos, who was quick-tempered, answered rather curtly and peremptorily, in a harsh voice: "Let the man sitting with Your Majesty on your couch explain it himself." The emperor at once took the remark into his heart like a dart of envy. But the blessed Sergios, wishing to soften the remark with his natural good sense, threw himself at Polyeuktos's feet and said: "Pray for me, holy father, for all these days I have been behaving improperly without realizing it." When the emperor asked, "Why did you do that?" he said: "Because that is how one who presides, especially over the Church, ought to act, and he should do nothing out of partiality." From then on he could never be persuaded to sit on the emperor's couch at all. 53. Now Stephen, the son of Romanos, rose up against his father. He took as counsellors Marianos, a former monk, Basil called Peteinos, and Manuel Kourtikes, and the other emperors were also privy to it. He saw that his father was worn down by great age and illness, and that he had settled the affairs of the empire by testament. Romanos had designated the Porphyrogennetos Constantine as first sovereign, and

after him, in second and third place, his own sons, and he had expressly secured himself against them: if they offended against the first emperor in any way, they would immediately be deposed from the throne. Yet Stephen wickedly brought him down from the palace, exiled him to the island of Prote and had him tonsured a monk. The Sole Reign of Constantine Porphyrogennetos

1. So Constantine, Romanos's son-in-law, was left as sole emperor on 20 December, in the third indiction, in the year 6454. He at once appointed Bardas Phokas magistros and domestic of the Scholai, Constantine commander of the navy, and certain capable men as generals. He made Peteinos patrician and count of the stable, and Kourtikes patrician and droungarios of the Watch. But God soon punished them for their lawless deed against the Lord's anointed: they were caught in treason, and each of them ended his life by a most pitiable death. 2. Forty days later Constantine the Porphyrogennetos grew suspicious of Stephen and Constantine, the brothers, fearing that they might do the same to him. This was likely, for if they had not spared their own father, how would they spare him? For it is said, "Bad company corrupts good morals"; what then of blood relatives? He feasted them and treated them kindly, and while the food was still in their mouths, men who had been made ready for the purpose seized them, made them clerics and banished them to the nearby islands. Shortly afterwards, overcome by unbearable grief, they asked to see their own father, who was now a monk. Smiling, he said to them: "I begot sons and raised them high, but they rejected me." They were then sent into exile as follows: Stephen to Prokonnesos, then to Rhodes, and after that to Mytilene; Constantine to Tenedos, and from there to Samothrace, where he plotted a revolt and was killed by those guarding him. The patriarch Theophylact took the imperial shoes from Michael, son of the emperor Christopher, and made him a cleric. Constantine likewise exiled Theophanes, patrician and parakoimomenos, along with George, protospatharios and cupbearer, and Thomas the primikerios. He had them flogged, shaved and paraded in a mock triumph, and then exiled them, because they had been caught watching for a chance to bring back [?]

3. In December, in the sixth indiction, a plot was formed to bring Stephen from the island back into the palace. When Michael Diabolinos informed against it, all the plotters were arrested. Some had their noses and ears cut off, others he subjected to unbearable flogging, and he set them on donkeys and paraded them [?]
4. On the fifteenth of the month of July, in the sixth indiction, the emperor Romanos died on the island, and his body was carried to the city and in his [?]

5. After the emperor Constantine had been left as sole ruler, he appointed his protovestiarios Basil, the natural son of Romanos, the emperor before him, by a concubine, to be patrician, parakoimomenos and chief minister over the senate. Basil was a sensible and learned man, and he served the emperor in all things well and fittingly. At that time the patriarch Theophylact also fell ill and, overcome by the illness, died, having governed the Church for twenty-four years. In his place the monk Polyeuktos, mentioned above, was ordained, an honourable and most holy man. 6. At that time, too, apostolic garments that had been hidden away in a corner of the city were revealed to the emperor. He took them up with all honour and with hymns of praise and laid them up as a treasure in the great church of the Holy Apostles. And the relics of Gregory the Theologian [?] were divided: some were placed in the sanctuary of the Holy Apostles, and the rest in the church of the holy martyr Anastasia. 7. The magistros and domestic of the Scholai, Bardas, called Phokas, had reached old age and could no longer bear the hardships, so the emperor removed him from the office of domestic and in his place promoted his son Nikephoros, patrician and strategos of the Anatolikon, to be domestic. In the same way he appointed the patrician Leo, Nikephoros' brother, strategos of the West. A great fire broke out near the church of Saint Thomas, so that the portico leading to the Iron Gate burned down. 8. Note that in the fourteenth year of the reign of Constantine Porphyrogenitus (for he reigned fifteen years) the emperor Basil was born, his grandson and the son of his son Romanos. When the Turks raided as far as the city at the feast of Easter, plundering all Thrace and taking much booty, the emperor at once sent the patrician and domestic of the Excubitors, Pothos Argyros, in pursuit with his tagma, together with the strategos of the Boukellarioi and those of the Opsikion and the Thrakesion. They fell on the Turks by night and slaughtered them, recovering both the booty and all the captives. 9. They say that at the birth of the Porphyrogenitus a bright star appeared for forty days, and that again, at his falling asleep and departure, a star appeared that gave a dim light. So he fell ill and died, having made his son Romanos emperor, and he was buried in the church of the Holy Apostles with his father the emperor Leo. In appearance he was tall in stature and fair of complexion, with fine, light-coloured eyes; he was hook-nosed, that is, aquiline, long-faced and long-necked, broad in the shoulders, fond of good food and of wine, and pleasant
in conversation. He lived fifty-five years, and died when his son Basil was one year old

his mother Helena and his wife Theophano. Then he immediately raised his father's men to the highest dignities, loaded them with gifts and sent them down from the palace. As his chief ministers and the first men of the senate he chose and preferred Joseph, patrician and droungarios of the fleet, whom shortly afterwards he also made parakoimomenos. He promoted the protospatharios John Choinos to be patrician and great hetaireiarch, and he appointed the protospatharios Sisinnios, formerly of the sakellion, eparch of the city, and shortly afterwards patrician and general logothete. His sisters Zoe, Theodora, [Agathe,] Theophano and Anna he brought down from the imperial apartments and took to the imperial residence called the Kanikleion, where Sophia Augusta, wife of the emperor Christopher, had also been tonsured; and after [?] days he assigned them to the Antiochos. Agathe he sent to the monastery founded by the emperor Romanos, his grandfather, and he ordered that they should be supplied with what they had been given in the palace. The domestic of the Scholai and patrician Nikephoros Phokas he honoured with the rank of magistros and sent to the East. Likewise he made Nikephoros' brother, the patrician Leo, magistros and domestic of the West [?]. He himself took his pleasure in hunting and the chase, living in luxury all the while. After his father's death he also had another son, whom he named Constantine; not long afterwards the boy was crowned by the patriarch Polyeuktos at the ambo of Hagia Sophia. The Augusta Helena lived with the emperor in the palace until she fell ill and died on the twelfth of the month of September. She was laid to rest in the monastery of her father, the emperor Romanos, in a sarcophagus near her father. 2. The emperor sent the magistros and domestic Nikephoros Phokas against Crete with a large army and a fitted-out fleet of warships and liquid fire. The island had formerly been under the Romans, but in the reign of Michael the Stammerer, father of Theophilos, it was seized by Saracens who had come up from Spain, because at that time the Roman armies were occupied with the

tyranny and revolt of the rebel Morothomas, Michael's comrade. As a result the island remained in their hands until the day when it was sacked again by Nikephoros, magistros and domestic [?], a period of 158 years. There were 2,000 chelandia with liquid fire, 1,000 dromons, and [?] cargo ships carrying grain and weapons of war. Nikephoros the domestic set out from the imperial city and, on reaching Phygela, took care that the whole fleet should be gathered together with him and come to anchor. They then reached the island quickly, and when they had disembarked from the ships they built a palisade and dug a deep trench. While they were encamped in this way against the island, a harsh winter set in with rain and frost, and the provisions ran out. The men of the army lost heart and wanted to return home, but Nikephoros, the most [?] commander, held them back with the sweetness of his words. When the emperor learned of the army's need, he sent them supplies of every kind of food. In the month of March, after fierce fighting and a hard battle, the Romans took the fortress. 3. In the month of October of the second year of Romanos' reign there was a shortage of wheat and barley in the city: wheat sold at four modioi to the nomisma, and barley at six. Not much time passed, and at once wheat went to eight modioi and barley to twelve. 4. In the month of March Basil Peteinos was accused by certain people of aspiring to the throne. He was sent into exile, where he died. When the emperor learned of the capture of Crete, he glorified God. Not long afterwards the domestic of the Scholai Nikephoros entered the city at the emperor's command. With the spoils and the captives he went on foot from his house to the Hippodrome, together with the emir of Crete, called the kouropalates [?], and all his relatives, all the Saracens being dressed in white robes. The magistros was granted great honours and rewards by the emperor. The emir received many gifts, gold and silver from the emperor and was allowed to live on estates with his children, but he was not admitted to the senate, because they refused to be baptized. The emperor Romanos then sent Nikephoros the magistros to the East again, against the braggart Chambdas. Going there, Nikephoros first took the fortress of Chelep, from which a great quantity of spoils was gathered.
